# Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI

Meng Luo¹ Zechen Bai¹ Shanqing Xu² Yanlin Li¹ Kaixin Li¹ Mengchen
Qian² Weifeng Lu³ Ran Zhang⁴ Yingtian Zou³ Ziyang Luo⁵ Wei
Chen² Hongzhan Lin^(1\*) ¹National University of Singapore ²Huazhong
University of Science and Technology ³Shanghai Jiao Tong
University ⁴Nanyang Technological University ⁵Hong Kong Baptist
University

\titlelogos

![[Uncaptioned image]](2610.29677v1/assets/nus_official.jpg)
![[Uncaptioned image]](2610.29677v1/assets/hust_emblem.png)

![[Uncaptioned image]](2610.29677v1/assets/ntu_official.png)
{physicalaifrontmatter}_Recursive self-improvement_ (RSI) describes a
system that improves not only its behavior but also the process by which
it improves. Recent digital agents test this idea by rewriting their own
code and checking each version with executable tests. Bringing these
mechanisms into the physical world requires learning from partial
observations through costly trials, while accounting for changing
operating conditions and potentially irreversible consequences. We
position RSI within robot learning and trace pathways from improving
robot capabilities to improving the processes that generate them. We
examine how physical experience can strengthen these improvement
mechanisms and when the resulting gains can support further
self-improvement of the mechanisms themselves. Gains carry forward only
when feedback addresses remaining learning needs, the receiving
component can use the change, its value survives changes in tasks or
hardware, and continued practice remains safe and affordable. Existing
studies, concentrated in manipulation, support behavioral improvement,
benefits to later learning, and procedure improvement. Some systems also
change the improver’s knowledge or tools, but the physical studies
reviewed here have yet to isolate gains attributable to recursion. We
synthesize these findings into evaluation principles and research
directions for machines that, trial by trial, safely improve the way
they improve.

## 1 Introduction

_Recursive self-improvement_ (RSI) describes a system that improves the
process by which it improves, not only its behavior. The idea goes back
to I. J. Good’s speculation about machines that design better
machines ([Good, 1966](#bib.bib87)) and to self-referential learners
such as the Gödel machine ([Schmidhuber, 2003](#bib.bib241)), and recent
digital agents have begun to approach it ([Chen et al.,
2026d](#bib.bib41)). STOP ([Zelikman et al., 2024](#bib.bib344)) applies
a program that improves code to its own source, and the Darwin Gödel
Machine ([Zhang et al., 2026c](#bib.bib350)) lets improved coding agents
modify themselves; both judge each candidate with executable tests. Yet
a system can get better at a task, and a fixed procedure can keep
producing better versions of it, without anything recursive happening.
RSI requires two further links
(Section [2.2](#S2.SS2 "2.2 Defining Recursive Self-Improvement ‣ 2 Foundations of Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")):
what the system retains from earlier improvements must make its next
revision better, and the _improver_, the component that revises the
learning procedure, must in turn use what it has gained to help produce
its own next improvement.

_Physical_ RSI asks the same question of systems that learn by acting in
the physical world, such as robots. Digital RSI supplies the mechanisms
(language models that write reward code or controllers, archives of
earlier variants, and automated experiment loops); physical RSI tests
how these mechanisms use physical experience and whether they hold under
physical constraints
(Figure [1](#S0.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")).
The physical setting changes the experimental conditions in four ways
(Table [1](#S1.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")).
First, physical outcome checks depend on sensors and task-specific
verifiers, people, or learned detectors whose reliability must be
established; even an automated grasp-success check can miss what it does
not sense, and an error in that judgment can be reinforced and then
executed on hardware. Second, every candidate costs robot time, resets,
supervision, and wear, so a revision must pay off within few trials.
Third, practice changes its own conditions: objects move, grippers wear,
calibration drifts, and rolling back software does not repair a damaged
object. Fourth, what can be improved extends beyond prompts and code to
controllers, dynamics models, and the interface to a particular body.
Each difference bears on the central question of RSI, whether what one
round of revision teaches the improver makes the next revision better.

Table 1: Experimental conditions of digital and physical
self-improvement. Digital examples include STOP, AlphaEvolve, and the
Darwin Gödel Machine.

Consider a robot arm that keeps missing the same grasp. The failure can
have several causes, and each calls for a change kept in a different
place; these places organize
Sections [3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Improving Policies, World Models, and Knowledge ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
and [3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Improving Learning Procedures ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI").
The robot’s _policy_, the learned controller that turns observations
into motor commands, may never produce the recovery motion; an expert
correction can teach it, as RECAP ([Physical Intelligence et al.,
2026](#bib.bib224)) learns from deployment experience and corrections
(Section [3.1.1](#S3.SS1.SSS1 "3.1.1 Policy Updates ‣ 3.1 Improving Policies, World Models, and Knowledge ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")).
The robot may mistake a light touch for a stable hold because its model
of contact is wrong; a _world model_ refitted to contact data can
correct the prediction and give the policy a place to practice, as in
PlayWorld ([Yin et al., 2026b](#bib.bib334))
(Section [3.1.2](#S3.SS1.SSS2 "3.1.2 World Models for Prediction and Practice ‣ 3.1 Improving Policies, World Models, and Knowledge ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")).
The robot may have recovered from this failure before without keeping
what worked; _external knowledge_, such as a saved recovery or program,
can be called the next time, as Zetta ([Ding et al., 2026](#bib.bib62))
grows code-based critics and recoveries around a frozen policy in
simulation
(Section [3.1.3](#S3.SS1.SSS3 "3.1.3 Memories, Skills, Code, and Runtimes ‣ 3.1 Improving Policies, World Models, and Knowledge ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")).
Finally, the robot may keep choosing the wrong kind of repair; then the
_learning procedure_ must change: which attempts to collect, how to
judge them, and how to turn them into updates
(Section [3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Improving Learning Procedures ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")).
Eureka ([Ma et al., 2024a](#bib.bib190)) rewrites reward code from
simulated training results, and ENPIRE ([Xiao et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib306)) lets coding agents modify the training
infrastructure from robot experiments. The first three routes improve
what the robot does; the fourth improves how it learns, and it is where
physical RSI would begin. Recursion would further require that knowledge
of why earlier repairs worked, which we call _repair knowledge_,
improves how the next procedure revision is made.
Figure [2](#S1.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
contrasts this route with applying a fixed training recipe to new
experience.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 2: Improving what the robot does and how it learns. On the left,
the learner improves under a fixed recipe and retains the change in its
policy, world model, or external knowledge. On the right, the improver
revises the learning procedure using retained repair knowledge; the
dashed return asks whether that knowledge improves how the next revision
is made (R1), and whether the improver, once improved, then helps
produce its own next improvement (R2). The bottom row lists the physical
limits behind the four conditions that let gains carry forward.

Our central argument is that physical experience can improve task
competence, the learning procedure, and the improver that revises this
procedure, and that four recurring conditions, each sharpened by the
physical setting, decide whether such gains carry forward. Each can
fail: the new signal may not address what the learner still lacks,
because sensing shows only part of a failure; the receiving component
may be unable to absorb it on its body; its value may not survive later
changes in behavior or hardware; or further practice may become unsafe
or unaffordable. For the grasping robot, this could mean collecting more
of the grasps it already makes well, refining a contact model that its
controller cannot use, relying on a fix that stops working once the
gripper is replaced, or practicing until the gripper wears out. A change
can improve execution and still fail to help later learning: added
autonomous data often yield modest gains that saturate and can even
regress ([Mirchandani et al., 2025](#bib.bib199)).

##### From learning actions to improving how learning happens.

Several research traditions supply pieces of this progression.
Self-supervised grasping showed that physical outcomes alone can
supervise behavior at scale, first by learning from tens of thousands of
real grasp attempts ([Pinto and Gupta, 2016](#bib.bib225)) and then
through large-scale real-robot reinforcement learning (RL) with
QT-Opt ([Kalashnikov et al., 2018](#bib.bib121)). Interactive imitation
learning, as in DAgger ([Ross et al., 2011](#bib.bib238)) and
HG-DAgger ([Kelly et al., 2019](#bib.bib123)), showed how an expert can
correct the learner in the states that the learner itself reaches.
Lifelong robot learning ([Thrun and Mitchell, 1995](#bib.bib268)) asks
how knowledge gained on earlier tasks can reduce the real-world
experimentation needed for later ones; model-based RL, from
Dyna ([Sutton, 1990](#bib.bib256)) and PILCO ([Deisenroth and Rasmussen,
2011](#bib.bib60)) to Dreamer ([Hafner et al., 2020](#bib.bib92)), asks
how recorded transitions can support practice inside a learned model;
and skill-based approaches, such as options ([Sutton et al.,
1999](#bib.bib258)) and the shared RoboEarth knowledge base ([Waibel
et al., 2011](#bib.bib273)), ask how an extended behavior can be stored
and called again. Each tradition widened what one learning episode can
pass on to the next.

Recent generalist and foundation-model-based systems widen both what can
change and what role the change plays. RoboCat ([Bousmalis et al.,
2024](#bib.bib28)) turns a policy adapted to a new task into a source of
training data for the next generalist, and SILVR ([Luo et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib182)) revises a video-based planner using its own
executions. In RoboCat, Eureka (in simulation), and ENPIRE, experience
reaches the machinery that produces future updates (a data collector, a
reward function, the training infrastructure) as well as the policy that
receives them. This brings the physical problem close to the
long-standing aspiration of learning to learn ([Thrun and Pratt,
1998](#bib.bib269)), and several reviewed systems already contain the
components that a demonstration of recursion would need. The open
question is how to realize that aspiration with limited trials,
imperfect sensing, and a body that changes over time.

##### Scope and related surveys.

Our scope is the improvement of policies, world models, memories,
skills, and the software procedures that update or use them, whenever
their evidence or evaluation is connected to physical action. We discuss
hardware change when it affects compatibility, maintenance, or continued
experimentation. Autonomous morphology design and physical
self-reconstruction are adjacent topics outside our scope.

Recent surveys cover neighboring ground
(Table [2](#S1.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Scope and related surveys. ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")).
Some focus on agents and embodiment: recursive self-improvement in AI
systems ([Chen et al., 2026d](#bib.bib41)), self-evolving agents ([Gao
et al., 2025](#bib.bib81)), weights versus executable skills as stores
of improvement ([Jena et al., 2026](#bib.bib118)), self-evolving
embodied AI ([Feng et al., 2026](#bib.bib77)) and humanoids ([Nguyen
et al., 2026](#bib.bib209)), and levels of physical recursive
self-improvement ([Zhou et al., 2026a](#bib.bib371)). Others analyze
world models for robot learning ([Hou et al., 2026](#bib.bib105)) and
manipulation ([Wang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib276)), joint world–action
models ([Lu et al., 2026b](#bib.bib181)), actionable simulators ([Chen
and Zhu, 2026](#bib.bib50)), verifiers for robot policies ([Wan et al.,
2026](#bib.bib275)), and physical AI broadly ([Xiang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib304)). Our organizing question is different: after a
change has been acquired, _who uses it next, and what does that use
improve?_ Component names alone cannot answer it, because two data
collectors with similar task success can yield training data of very
different value; a more accurate predictor can still produce less useful
training data for a policy; and the same kind of retrieved memory can
change either how a program is repaired or how an outcome is judged.

Table 2: Closely related reviews and the complementary focus of this
review.

The review makes three connected contributions. First, it positions RSI
within robot learning by separating method paradigms and problem
settings (from reinforcement learning and meta-learning to AutoML) from
a ladder of claims (behavioral improvement, later-learning benefit,
procedure improvement, and the two links of recursion), each defined by
the comparison that would establish it. It organizes physical
self-improvement along that ladder according to where experience leaves
its change and which decision of the learning procedure it revises,
showing that data volume and component accuracy are unreliable proxies
for progress. Second, it separates mechanisms that change an improver’s
knowledge or tools from evidence that the improver has improved:
existing studies support the first three claims, while recursive gains
still need dedicated verification. It reviews digital precedents and
physical boundary cases and specifies a two-round experiment that could
isolate the recursive relation, together with its controls and an
estimate of its hardware cost;
Table [13](#S4.T13 "Table 13 ‣ 4.1 Measuring Improvement ‣ 4 Challenges and Future Directions for Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
records where the reviewed studies stand on each claim. Third, it names
the four breakdowns above as recurring conditions (_informative
feedback_, _usability_, _robustness to distribution shift_, and
_continued practice_) and shows how each fails and which capability
would restore it. Four research questions organize the review.

## 2 Foundations of Physical RSI

We follow every system in this review along one path: from experience,
to a retained change, to the change’s next use. Later sections use this
path to work out when a gain survives another round, without assuming a
common architecture.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 3: The review at a glance. Illustrations in (b) show the four
grasp breakdowns from
Section [1](#S1 "1 Introduction ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI").

### 2.1 Learning to Act

A few groups of ideas are enough to follow the rest of the review. We
introduce them with the running example of the robot that keeps missing
a grasp.

##### Policies.

A _policy_ is the controller that maps what the robot currently observes
(camera images, joint angles, force readings, and possibly a language
instruction) to its next motor command; for the grasping robot, it turns
a view of the object into the next movement of the arm and gripper. In
the systems reviewed here, policies are usually neural networks.
_Generalist_ policies are trained on large collections of robot data
spanning many tasks, as in RT-1 ([Brohan et al., 2023b](#bib.bib30)),
and sometimes many robot bodies, or _embodiments_, as in Octo ([Octo
Model Team et al., 2024](#bib.bib212)). A _vision-language model_ (VLM)
reads images and text and outputs text; robot systems often use one to
propose goals or to judge whether an attempt succeeded. A
_vision-language-action_ (VLA) model is a generalist policy built on a
pretrained VLM, so that it reads images and an instruction and outputs
actions; RT-2 ([Brohan et al., 2023a](#bib.bib29)), OpenVLA ([Kim
et al., 2024](#bib.bib127)), and $`\pi_{0}`$ ([Black et al.,
2025](#bib.bib25)) are examples. Many recent policies output a short
sequence of future actions at once, called an _action chunk_.

##### Learning from demonstrations.

The simplest way to obtain a policy is _imitation learning_ from
demonstrations, which are often recorded while a person teleoperates the
robot ([Argall et al., 2009](#bib.bib13)). In _behavior cloning_ (BC),
the policy is trained to reproduce the demonstrated action in each
recorded situation. BC learns only from recorded situations, so its
small errors can compound: if the gripper drifts slightly off the object
into a state that no demonstration covers, the policy may have no good
action to take. Interactive methods such as DAgger ([Ross et al.,
2011](#bib.bib238)) address this by asking an expert what to do in the
situations that the learner itself reaches. In practice, a person often
takes over when the robot errs, and these _interventions_ supply
corrective training data.

##### Learning from rewards.

In _reinforcement learning_ (RL) ([Sutton and Barto, 2018](#bib.bib257);
[Kober et al., 2013](#bib.bib128)), the robot instead tries actions and
receives a _reward_ that scores the outcome, for example 1 for a stable
grasp and 0 otherwise. On a real robot, rewards do not arrive
automatically: a person, a hand-written check, or a learned _reward
model_, such as a success detector, must judge each attempt. We call a
component that supplies such judgments for learning an _evaluator_.
Because rewards are often sparse and delayed, many methods learn a
_value function_, or _critic_, that predicts how much future reward to
expect; some systems use the word critic more loosely for any component,
learned or hand-written, that scores behavior. The _advantage_ of an
action measures how much better it is than what the policy would
typically do in the same situation. _Off-policy_ methods can learn from
experience collected by earlier versions of the policy or by other
sources, which they keep in a _replay buffer_. On hardware, every trial
costs time, supervision, wear, and a _reset_ that returns the scene to a
usable starting state, so the source of the reward and the number of
available trials become central resources.

##### Improving an existing policy.

Large pretrained policies are rarely retrained from scratch. They are
_fine-tuned_, or post-trained, on new data. A small _residual_ policy
can add corrections on top of the actions of a frozen base policy, such
as a slight change to the angle at which the gripper approaches the
object. _Distillation_ trains one policy to imitate another, for example
to fold a specialist’s behavior back into a generalist. When a policy
learns a sequence of tasks, it can forget earlier ones, a problem
studied in continual learning ([Parisi et al., 2019](#bib.bib221));
_replaying_ stored data from earlier tasks is a common protection.

##### Models of the world.

A _world model_, or dynamics model, predicts what will happen after an
action, for instance the next camera image or the next object
positions ([Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018](#bib.bib91); [Hafner et al.,
2020](#bib.bib92)). The grasping robot’s contact model is one example:
it predicts whether a touch will become a stable hold. A robot can use
such a model to _plan_, by imagining the outcomes of candidate actions,
or to generate _imagined experience_ on which a policy is trained. A
physics simulator is a hand-built model of this kind; a learned world
model is fitted to recorded robot data and can be wrong in ways that a
policy may learn to exploit.

##### Improvements outside the weights.

Not every improvement is stored in network weights. A system can keep
_memories_ of earlier episodes, maintain a library of callable
*skills* ([Sutton et al., 1999](#bib.bib258)), or write _programs_ that
compose perception and control functions ([Liang et al.,
2023](#bib.bib159)). Large language models are increasingly used to
write such code or to revise reward functions ([Ma et al.,
2024a](#bib.bib190)).

##### Simulation and hardware.

Results come either from simulation benchmarks or from hardware
experiments on physical robots, and training in simulation before
deployment on hardware is called _sim-to-real_ transfer.
Section [2.4](#S2.SS4 "2.4 Facing Physical Limits ‣ 2 Foundations of Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
discusses what each setting can establish.

### 2.2 Defining Recursive Self-Improvement

##### Where experience leaves a change.

We consider loops in which experience produces a retained change that
affects later attempts or learning. Human demonstration, correction,
reset, or approval can remain part of the loop: automation concerns who
makes each decision, whereas learning concerns whether experience
changes it
(Table [17](#A1.T17 "Table 17 ‣ Appendix A Extended Landscape of Physical Self-Improvement ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
in
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Extended Landscape of Physical Self-Improvement ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")).
A failed update can also be informative by showing where this connection
breaks.

Generic pretraining without a subsequent experience–update–use
comparison serves as background, as does adaptation confined to a single
attempt. Rapid Motor Adaptation ([Kumar et al., 2021](#bib.bib131)), for
example, infers current conditions from recent history without retaining
the adaptation. Zeva’s interaction memory is a boundary case: it carries
across retries within an episode but not across episodes or learning
rounds. Simulation-only and formal studies supply enabling mechanisms,
while meta-learning, AutoML, and digital agents supply precedents
(Section [2.3](#S2.SS3 "2.3 Relating RSI to Robot Learning ‣ 2 Foundations of Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI"));
direct evidence about physical RSI must come from physical systems.

A retained change can serve four uses
(Figure [4](#S2.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Where experience leaves a change. ‣ 2.2 Defining Recursive Self-Improvement ‣ 2 Foundations of Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")).
It can choose or execute actions, predict outcomes or supply practice,
support reuse (for example, calling a saved recovery or consulting
guidance for a new program), or change how later data are collected,
judged, and turned into updates. These uses are usually carried by
policies, world models, external knowledge, and learning procedures,
respectively
(Sections [3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Improving Policies, World Models, and Knowledge ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
and [3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Improving Learning Procedures ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")).
They can overlap: a policy can collect training data, a model can judge
outcomes, and a memory can guide an updater. Each study is discussed
mainly under the use its experiment tests, regardless of whether its
authors call it self-evolving or recursively self-improving.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 4: Where a retained change is kept and how it is used. Each row
follows the grasp example from physical experience to the retained
change and its immediate use; the italic line names the use. Dashed tags
mark secondary handoffs into the learning procedure.

##### Learner, learning procedure, and improver.

The learner acquires task capabilities; the _learning procedure_
determines what experience to collect, how to judge it, and how to
construct updates. An _improver_ proposes or selects revisions of that
procedure. It may be a person, a fixed rule, a search process, or a
learned component, with knowledge in memory, weights, code, or prompts.
Figure [2](#S1.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
separates the two levels: the learner improves under a fixed recipe,
whereas the improver revises the recipe itself.

In the grasp example, adding a corrected grasp to the training data is a
_repair_, an update made in response to an observed failure or
limitation. The rule choosing which failed grasps need correction
belongs to the learning procedure; whoever devises or changes that rule
is the improver. The object being changed determines the role: an editor
of task skills or data belongs to the procedure, whereas an editor of
rewards, evaluators, collection rules, or update-generating training
code acts as an improver.

##### From better behavior to recursion.

We distinguish four claims
(Table [3](#S2.T3 "Table 3 ‣ From better behavior to recursion. ‣ 2.2 Defining Recursive Self-Improvement ‣ 2 Foundations of Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")),
and evidence for an earlier claim does not establish a later one.
_Behavioral improvement_ means better execution under a common task
test. A _later-learning benefit_ means that retained data, weights,
models, skills, or code help a subsequent learner. _Procedure
improvement_ means that a revised collector, evaluator, editor, or
updater teaches better than its earlier version. This comparison
requires _matched learners_, which differ only in the component under
test and share starting conditions, resources, and evaluation protocol
(Figure [8](#S3.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ 3.2 Improving Learning Procedures ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")).

We operationalize _recursive self-improvement_ through two further
links, which this review uses as empirical criteria for attributing a
gain to recursion. First (R1), _repair knowledge_ retained from earlier
repairs must improve the improver: on new failures, its procedures must
teach matched learners better than those produced by its earlier
version. Second (R2), the improver, once improved, must help produce its
own next improvement: given the same new repair histories, a
self-revision proposed using its acquired knowledge must yield an
improver that outperforms both the improver it revised and a revision of
that same improver proposed with the acquired knowledge frozen. A fixed
improver can repeatedly improve procedures without satisfying either
link; an external designer’s growing expertise does not establish
system-level recursion either.
Section [3.3](#S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1 "What would count as a better improver. ‣ 3.3 Improving the Improver ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
develops the grasp example. A concurrent survey grades physical RSI by
whether an update changes capabilities or the improvement procedure and
whether its gain holds on the same or on other tasks, reserving its top
level for an independently verified recursive gain ([Zhou et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib371)); the claims here are instead defined by the
comparison that would establish each. The name is shared by other
concurrent work. PhysRSI-eval ([Li et al., 2026j](#bib.bib156)) applies
it to agents with frozen weights that revise code, tools, and notes
after each graded attempt, and Physical RSI 1.0 ([MMLab & PhysicalRSI
contributors, 2026](#bib.bib200)) names a system in which a multimodal
foundation model revises the harness through which a robot acts. We read
these works, like any other, by the comparisons they report; a name does
not establish either link. In symbols, write $`L`$ for a learner,
$`J(L)`$ for its outcome under a protected success evaluation, and
$`P=(c,e,d,u)`$ for a learning procedure whose components choose what
experience to collect, evaluate outcomes, select the training data, and
apply the update rule; $`P(L)`$ is the learner that $`P`$ produces from
$`L`$ under a fixed budget. Behavioral improvement means
$`J(L^{\prime})>J(L)`$. Procedures are compared from a common starting
learner $`L_{0}`$ with matched resources and evaluation, and we write
$`J(P)=J(P(L_{0}))`$: procedure improvement means
$`J(P^{\prime})>J(P)`$, and a later-learning benefit from a retained
artifact $`A`$ means $`J(P(L_{0};A))>J(P(L_{0}))`$, where $`P(L_{0};A)`$
is trained with access to $`A`$. An improver $`I`$ maps failure
histories $`F`$ to a procedure $`I(F)`$. Write $`I^{K}`$ for the
improver with knowledge $`K`$, $`K_{0}`$ and $`K_{1}`$ for its knowledge
before and after earlier repairs, and $`\rho_{K}(I,H)`$ for the improver
obtained when a self-revision of $`I`$ is proposed from repair histories
$`H`$ with knowledge $`K`$ available. On new failures $`F`$, held out
from everything the improver has learned from and from $`H`$, the two
links require

|     |     |                                                                                                                                                      |     |
| --- | --- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- |
|     | R1: | $`\displaystyle J\bigl(I^{K_{1}}(F)\bigr)>J\bigl(I^{K_{0}}(F)\bigr),`$                                                                               |     |
|     | R2: | $`\displaystyle J\bigl(\rho_{K_{1}}(I^{K_{1}},H)(F)\bigr)>\max\bigl\{J\bigl(I^{K_{1}}(F)\bigr),\ J\bigl(\rho_{K_{0}}(I^{K_{1}},H)(F)\bigr)\bigr\}.`$ |     |

In R1, the right-hand side is the frozen-knowledge control. In R2, the
first term requires the successor to improve on its parent, so a
revision that changes nothing cannot pass; the second revises the same
parent with the acquired knowledge frozen and so isolates what that
knowledge contributes to the revision. Withholding the acquired
knowledge while keeping the same parent is straightforward when that
knowledge resides in a memory snapshot, code, or prompts; when it is
stored in the improver’s weights, the R2 control needs a design of its
own.

Table 3: The comparison each claim requires. All comparisons use matched
learners and budgets; in R2, the updated improver is revised once with
its acquired knowledge and once with that knowledge frozen, and the
successor must also beat the updated improver itself (inequalities in
Section [2.2](#S2.SS2 "2.2 Defining Recursive Self-Improvement ‣ 2 Foundations of Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")).

##### How far a result supports recursion.

For R1 and R2, we distinguish _mechanism only_, where machinery could
change the improver; an _uncontrolled result_, consistent with a link
but without a control that withholds only what was acquired; and a
_controlled result_, which tests that contribution with matched learners
and budgets
(Section [4.4](#S4.SS4.SSS0.Px6 "How to test recursion. ‣ 4.4 Making Improvement Recursive ‣ 4 Challenges and Future Directions for Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")).
The claim and its level of support are separate.

Two controls answer different questions. A frozen-knowledge control
withholds acquired repair knowledge while retaining the improver,
testing that knowledge’s contribution to the procedures produced (R1) or
the self-revision proposed (R2). A fixed-improver control keeps the
initial improver while the rest of the system improves. A gain over it
shows that revising the improver contributes to later improvement,
bearing on R2, but does not identify which acquired knowledge caused the
revision.

##### What lets gains carry forward.

Four conditions recur across these claims. _Informative feedback_
distinguishes the remaining learning need. _Usability_ means that the
receiving component can represent, optimize, and execute the change.
_Robustness to distribution shift_ asks whether the change stays useful
as the policy, model, task, or hardware changes, including changes
caused by improvement itself. _Continued practice_ asks whether another
informative trial remains safe and affordable. These four conditions
overlap and serve as diagnostic lenses rather than independently
validated constructs.
Section [4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Accumulating Improvement ‣ 4 Challenges and Future Directions for Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
examines their failures, and
Figure [3](#S2.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 2 Foundations of Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
connects these conditions to the uses and claims above.

### 2.3 Relating RSI to Robot Learning

Reinforcement learning and meta-learning already let robots improve from
experience and learn how to learn. Self-training, continual learning,
and automated machine learning (AutoML) let systems learn from their own
outputs, keep learning across tasks, or search for better training
recipes. It is therefore fair to ask what RSI adds. These are method
paradigms or problem settings, which say how an update is computed or
what it must cope with, whereas the claims of
Section [2.2](#S2.SS2 "2.2 Defining Recursive Self-Improvement ‣ 2 Foundations of Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
say what an experiment shows to have changed. An RSI system may use any
of them to revise any of its components, so the categories overlap
rather than exclude one another: RSI is not a further paradigm after
meta-learning but a level of improvement that a system built with any of
them might reach
(Table [4](#S2.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 2.3 Relating RSI to Robot Learning ‣ 2 Foundations of Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")).

Table 4: How learning paradigms and problem settings relate to the
claims of
Section [2.2](#S2.SS2 "2.2 Defining Recursive Self-Improvement ‣ 2 Foundations of Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI").
The last four columns show how each approach can support each claim; the
R1, R2 column concerns whether the improvement mechanism itself
improves.

##### Reinforcement learning.

Standard RL improves a policy under an objective and update mechanism
chosen before training ([Sutton and Barto, 2018](#bib.bib257)). Run
repeatedly on hardware, as in HIL-SERL ([Luo et al., 2025](#bib.bib184))
and RECAP ([Physical Intelligence et al., 2026](#bib.bib224)), it yields
behavioral improvement, and its data or policy can supply a
later-learning benefit. RL loops can also be nested inside an outer
optimization over part of the learning procedure. Eureka searches over
reward programs using the RL training results they produce ([Ma et al.,
2024a](#bib.bib190)), and meta-gradient RL adapts the return while the
agent learns ([Xu et al., 2018](#bib.bib320)). LPG discovers an update
rule ([Oh et al., 2020](#bib.bib213)), and DiscoRL learns such a rule
across many agents and environments and applies it to unseen
benchmarks ([Oh et al., 2025](#bib.bib214)). These loops target
procedure improvement, while the outer search itself stays fixed.
DERL ([Cheng et al., 2025](#bib.bib51)) departs from this on text-based
and mathematical reasoning tasks: it trains its reward proposer by
policy gradient on the validation success of the inner policies, so the
search learns from its own trials, while the rule that trains the
proposer stays fixed. In the grasp example, RL that tunes the grasp
under a fixed slip penalty improves behavior, whereas a search that
revises the slip penalty changes the procedure; further rounds of the
first kind do not become the second.

##### Self-training.

Many systems called self-improving train on their own outputs. In
self-training such as Noisy Student ([Xie et al., 2020](#bib.bib309)), a
teacher trained on labeled data labels unlabeled data, and a student
trained on both becomes the next teacher. Expert Iteration ([Anthony
et al., 2017](#bib.bib12)) and STaR ([Zelikman et al.,
2022](#bib.bib343)) apply the same pattern to search and reasoning, and
RoboCat ([Bousmalis et al., 2024](#bib.bib28)) applies it to robot data
collection. Each round improves behavior and helps the next learner
through the data it generates, while the recipe that generates, labels
or filters, and trains on the data stays fixed. When the model also
judges its own outputs, as in Self-Rewarding Language Models ([Yuan
et al., 2024](#bib.bib342)), the evaluator changes with training, but
the judging prompt and the training recipe do not.

##### Continual learning.

Continual, or lifelong, learning asks how a learner that meets a
sequence of tasks can reuse what it learned on earlier ones ([Thrun and
Mitchell, 1995](#bib.bib268)) without forgetting them ([Parisi et al.,
2019](#bib.bib221)). Backward and forward transfer ([Lopez-Paz and
Ranzato, 2017](#bib.bib176)) measure how learning one task changes
performance on earlier and later ones. Backward transfer thus measures
retention, whereas forward transfer as defined there is performance on a
new task before training on it; LIBERO ([Liu et al.,
2023a](#bib.bib164)), a benchmark of sequential robot manipulation
tasks, instead scores forward transfer by success on each new task
averaged over its training, which is closer to a later-learning benefit.
Replay, regularization, and other protections against forgetting are
usually chosen by designers, so continual learning defines a setting
that an RSI system must also handle
(Section [4.2](#S4.SS2.SSS0.Px4 "When knowledge is lost or misused. ‣ 4.2 Accumulating Improvement ‣ 4 Challenges and Future Directions for Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI"))
rather than a way of improving the improver.

##### Meta-learning.

Meta-learning trains over many tasks so that new tasks are learned
faster ([Thrun and Pratt, 1998](#bib.bib269)), and what it learns
decides which claim it can support. An initialization from which a few
gradient steps solve a new task, as in MAML ([Finn et al.,
2017](#bib.bib79)), is an acquired artifact and supports a
later-learning benefit. Other methods learn part of the learning
procedure: recurrent policies whose activations carry out
adaptation ([Duan et al., 2016](#bib.bib68); [Wang et al.,
2016](#bib.bib278)), a dynamics prior that adapts online, as in
GrBAL ([Nagabandi et al., 2019](#bib.bib203)), learned
optimizers ([Andrychowicz et al., 2016](#bib.bib9)), and evolved or
learned losses ([Houthooft et al., 2018](#bib.bib106); [Yu et al.,
2018](#bib.bib337); [Bechtle et al., 2021](#bib.bib22)). When a learner
guided by such a part learns better than a matched learner guided by the
original, the comparison supports procedure improvement. LMPC ([Liang
et al., 2024](#bib.bib160)) is a boundary case: it fine-tunes the model
that writes reward code on past teaching sessions so that later teaching
needs fewer turns, but that code drives a model-predictive controller
directly rather than a training run, so the gain lies in how behavior is
constructed. The outer meta-training procedure that produces the part (a
gradient loop, an evolutionary search, or a fine-tuning recipe) is
specified by its designers and is not changed by the revisions it
produces, so learning reaches the procedure but not the process that
produces it.

##### Automated machine learning.

AutoML searches over architectures, hyperparameters, and training
pipelines ([Hutter et al., 2019](#bib.bib112)), and AutoML-Zero extends
the search to learning algorithms ([Real et al., 2020](#bib.bib230)); a
found configuration that teaches matched learners better supports
procedure improvement. Some searchers learn from their own record: the
controller of neural architecture search ([Zoph and Le,
2017](#bib.bib379)) is trained with reinforcement learning on the
validation accuracy of the architectures it generates. Because it edits
the learner rather than the rules for collecting, judging, or updating,
it is a learned part of the procedure, like the skill editor of
PRACTICE ([Bai et al., 2026](#bib.bib18)), and the rule that trains it
stays fixed.

##### Where recursion adds a requirement.

RSI moves the process that produces revisions inside as well, as the two
links of
Section [2.2](#S2.SS2 "2.2 Defining Recursive Self-Improvement ‣ 2 Foundations of Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
require. The requirement is self-referential, as in the Gödel
machine ([Schmidhuber, 2003](#bib.bib241)), STOP ([Zelikman et al.,
2024](#bib.bib344)), the Darwin Gödel Machine ([Zhang et al.,
2026c](#bib.bib350)), and Gödel Agent ([Yin et al., 2025](#bib.bib335)),
which let the improving process act on its own code. Generalized Agent
Iteration places iterative policy improvement and RSI in one formal
framework, in which whether the improvement mechanism sits inside the
agent separates the two, and whether the evaluation standard is grounded
outside it decides whether goals can drift ([Tang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib264)). The criterion is therefore which component changes
with the revision history, not whether some outer recipe stays fixed. In
the meta-learning and AutoML methods above, the component that produces
revisions of the learning procedure does not change; an improver
fine-tuned by a fixed recipe on its own repair histories does change and
can satisfy R1, which the frozen-knowledge comparison of
Section [4.4](#S4.SS4.SSS0.Px6 "How to test recursion. ‣ 4.4 Making Improvement Recursive ‣ 4 Challenges and Future Directions for Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
tests. Conversely, an improver whose code changes in every round
satisfies neither link if the changes come from a designer or from a
search that learns nothing from earlier rounds.

### 2.4 Facing Physical Limits

Table [1](#S1.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
lists the terms we use to judge how closely a study is tied to physical
experience. Hardware interaction connects learning directly to physical
consequences, but a consequence still needs a diagnosis and a reliable
judge. A binary failure label on a grasp may not distinguish pose error
from slip, whereas force measurements or contact history may separate
the two. Simulation, learned prediction, and formal checks represent
selected consequences whose adequacy must be tested at the decision they
support. Simulation is cheap and repeatable but omits some physical
effects, whereas hardware captures real contact, sensing, and wear but
allows few trials, so the two settings support different conclusions
about cost, transfer, and the comparisons a study can afford.

Because practice changes its own conditions
(Section [1](#S1 "1 Introduction ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")),
returning to a usable starting state may require a reset policy or human
assistance; early work on autonomous real-world RL already named resets,
onboard perception, and rewards without instrumentation as the
ingredients that continued learning needs ([Zhu et al.,
2020](#bib.bib378)). Moving knowledge to another robot adds a further
gap, because reuse across bodies needs compatible coordinates, timing,
sensing, and reachable effects. A study’s connection to physical
experience is therefore a matter of degree. It depends on the _success
evaluation_ (who or what judges whether an attempt succeeded), on
interaction coverage and recoverability, and on whether successive
trials remain comparable. The success evaluation may rely on the same
evaluator that supplied the learning signal or on one independent of it,
a difference that
Section [4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Measuring Improvement ‣ 4 Challenges and Future Directions for Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
shows to matter.
Table [1](#S1.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
contrasts these conditions with those of digital self-improvement,
Section [4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Keeping Improvement Safe ‣ 4 Challenges and Future Directions for Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
develops their consequences for continued learning, and
Table [18](#A1.T18 "Table 18 ‣ Appendix A Extended Landscape of Physical Self-Improvement ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
in
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Extended Landscape of Physical Self-Improvement ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
shows what evidence each robot domain contributes.

These conditions weigh on each paradigm of
Section [2.3](#S2.SS3 "2.3 Relating RSI to Robot Learning ‣ 2 Foundations of Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
in a different place. Meta-learning needs a distribution of training
tasks, and on hardware every sampled task costs trials, resets, and
supervision; domain-adaptive meta-learning meta-trains on previously
collected human and robot demonstrations, and LMPC collected its
training data in simulation. Eureka and DrEureka run their reward search
in simulation, where many candidates can be trained in parallel, and
DrEureka then deploys the resulting policy on hardware ([Ma et al.,
2024b](#bib.bib191)). For RSI, the bottleneck shifts to revision
histories: an improver learns from them, and each entry needs at least
one learning round judged by physical trials, so these histories
accumulate more slowly than the task samples of meta-learning or the
transitions of RL, and no executable test settles whether a revision
helped. Simulation, stored traces, and learned models can screen
candidate revisions before hardware trials, but their adequacy for that
screening is itself a claim to test
(Section [4.4](#S4.SS4.SSS0.Px7 "What the test must control. ‣ 4.4 Making Improvement Recursive ‣ 4 Challenges and Future Directions for Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")).

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

digital tasks.

Most comparisons in this review run in simulation, and the benchmarks
differ in what they stress
(Table [5](#S2.T5 "Table 5 ‣ 2.5 Benchmarking Self-Improvement ‣ 2 Foundations of Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")).
LIBERO ([Liu et al., 2023a](#bib.bib164)) supplies sequential
manipulation suites, and LIBERO-PRO ([Zhou et al., 2025b](#bib.bib372))
perturbs manipulated objects, initial states, task instructions, and
environments to test whether behavior depends on the original cues;
LIBERO-Plus ([Fei et al., 2025](#bib.bib76)) varies seven factors,
including camera viewpoint, initial robot state, and sensor noise.
RoboCasa ([Nasiriany et al., 2024](#bib.bib206)) broadens household task
coverage, and RoboTwin 2.0 ([Chen et al., 2025c](#bib.bib44)) and
RoboDojo ([Chen et al., 2026g](#bib.bib45)) cover bimanual manipulation.
VLABench ([Zhang et al., 2025d](#bib.bib358)) and Meta-World ([Yu
et al., 2019](#bib.bib338)) supply further manipulation suites, and
SIMPLER ([Li et al., 2024](#bib.bib153)) mirrors real robot setups for
policy evaluation. Navigation studies use Habitat ([Savva et al.,
2019](#bib.bib240)) and R2R-CE ([Krantz et al., 2020](#bib.bib129)), and
household agents use EmbodiedBench ([Yang et al., 2025](#bib.bib329)).
Except for LIBERO’s lifelong protocol, which scores transfer and
forgetting along a task sequence, these suites test a system at one
point in time, and a claim about improvement across rounds still needs a
protocol on top that fixes what carries over between rounds and what
stays held out
(Section [4.2](#S4.SS2.SSS0.Px4 "When knowledge is lost or misused. ‣ 4.2 Accumulating Improvement ‣ 4 Challenges and Future Directions for Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")).
A recent benchmark prototype moves in this direction: it provides no
in-domain demonstrations, carries experience over between requests
within a deployment, and names how quickly an agent becomes competent in
a deployment as a quantity of interest ([Cai et al., 2026](#bib.bib34)).
PhysRSI-eval ([Li et al., 2026j](#bib.bib156)) fixes what carries over
between rounds, in simulation. Six model-and-configuration systems
revise a persistent workspace of code, tools and notes with frozen
weights, for up to 17 graded rounds on each of 18 RoboDojo tasks, and
each system is scored on five axes: first-attempt score, how early gains
appear, attained score, physical budget saved, and the share of
first-round failures later solved. The axes need not agree: Claude Opus
5.5 attains a higher score than GPT-6.1 Sol but scores lower on gain
timing and budget saved. In a six-task ablation with GPT-6 Astra,
withholding all information from earlier rounds lowers success over
rounds 4–6 from 15 of 36 attempts to 3 of 36.

A second group of benchmarks targets the components on which
self-improvement relies. FailBench ([Navasardyan et al.,
2026](#bib.bib207)) tests success detectors on 2,197 real and simulated
manipulation attempts, where the best of 13 VLM detectors reaches 0.77
balanced accuracy. CaliBench ([Sadeghi et al., 2026](#bib.bib239)) tests
whether the outcome frequencies of video world models are calibrated.
MC-EvoBench ([Song et al., 2026a](#bib.bib248)) fixes the controls that
a transfer claim needs, and RLE-Bench ([Ma et al., 2026](#bib.bib186))
holds out robustness perturbations that coding agents cannot query.
RoboCoach-Bench ([Lei et al., 2026](#bib.bib143)) collects 32 simulated
tasks for agents that write and revise training code. Digital benchmarks
of recursive self-improvement isolate related questions.
PAST-Bench ([Xue et al., 2026a](#bib.bib321)) turns retained experience
on and off across ordered task sequences, and RSIBench-Data ([Meng
et al., 2026a](#bib.bib196)) has agents revise training-data strategies
for a fixed model. RSIGym ([Meng et al., 2026b](#bib.bib197)) measures
the fraction of the remaining performance gap that agents close across
benchmarks.

Hardware evaluations instead use task suites built by each study, and
their budgets vary widely, from a handful of trials per task, as in
PhysEvo’s 25 trials over five real tasks ([Tian et al.,
2026](#bib.bib270)), to hundreds of evaluation episodes, as in the more
than 600 pairwise episodes of RoboArena ([Atreya et al.,
2025](#bib.bib15)). Most controlled downstream comparisons concern
manipulation; navigation, locomotion, flight, and robotic laboratories
support particular mechanisms without testing each condition across
robot bodies
(Table [18](#A1.T18 "Table 18 ‣ Appendix A Extended Landscape of Physical Self-Improvement ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")).
Simulation results support mechanism comparisons at scale, whereas
hardware results show what survives real contact, sensing, and resets
(Section [2.4](#S2.SS4 "2.4 Facing Physical Limits ‣ 2 Foundations of Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")).
Because tasks, trial counts, and metrics differ, results are compared
within each study rather than across studies;
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Reported Outcomes and Experimental Context ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
records the settings behind selected numbers.

Most studies report success rate, the fraction of trials that reach a
task-defined goal as judged by a person, a scripted check, or a learned
detector. Some give partial credit for progress through task stages,
which needs a different statistical model than binary success. Others
add efficiency during execution, such as cycle time in HIL-SERL ([Luo
et al., 2025](#bib.bib184)) or throughput in RECAP ([Physical
Intelligence et al., 2026](#bib.bib224)).

Learning efficiency is reported as the time, episodes, or supervision
needed to reach a level of performance. ConRFT ([Chen et al.,
2025d](#bib.bib48)) reaches 96.3% average success on eight real tasks
after 45–90 minutes of online fine-tuning, and VLAC ([Zhai et al.,
2025](#bib.bib345)) raises real success from about 30% to 90% within 200
episodes. ENPIRE ([Xiao et al., 2026b](#bib.bib306)) reports the time
its robot fleet needs to reach a target, and LMPC ([Liang et al.,
2024](#bib.bib160)) counts chat turns per successful teaching session.

_Retention_ asks whether earlier competence survives later learning or
deployment, and a later-learning benefit on a new task is _forward
transfer_. ACCRUE ([Kim et al., 2026](#bib.bib126)) reports transfer as
a cut in real-robot training time for later tasks, CIDER ([Li et al.,
2026d](#bib.bib148)) reports forward transfer of an accumulated policy,
and MC-EvoBench sets out the controls that such a claim needs.

Resource use is counted in robot hours, demonstrations, interventions,
compute, or model tokens. CARD ([Sun et al., 2024](#bib.bib255)) needs
about 14K tokens per task against about 663K for Eureka, and ENPIRE’s
fleet scaling shortens the time to target at lower per-robot utilization
and faster-than-linear token growth; because studies count different
parts of this work, their costs are not directly comparable
(Section [4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Measuring Improvement ‣ 4 Challenges and Future Directions for Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")).
\physicalaisectionaccentPAIBlue

## 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI

This section reviews physical self-improvement by what a system actually
changes, following the ladder of
Section [2.2](#S2.SS2 "2.2 Defining Recursive Self-Improvement ‣ 2 Foundations of Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI").
Section [3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Improving Policies, World Models, and Knowledge ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
covers changes to the learner $`L`$, kept in policies, world models, or
external knowledge; a policy trained with relabeled targets, a reward,
or an optimization algorithm belongs there, because those rules stay
fixed.
Section [3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Improving Learning Procedures ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
covers changes to the rules themselves, the learning procedure $`P`$
that collects, judges, and updates, and
Section [3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Improving the Improver ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
covers changes to the improver $`I^{K}`$ that revises that procedure
(notation of
Section [2.2](#S2.SS2 "2.2 Defining Recursive Self-Improvement ‣ 2 Foundations of Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")).
Section [3.4](#S3.SS4 "3.4 Closing the Recursive Loop ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
adds no fourth component: it asks whether these layers close into a
recursive relation, in which the improver, once improved, helps produce
its own next improvement. A system that serves several roles is
discussed mainly where its experiment tests it, with cross-references
elsewhere;
Table [11](#S3.T11 "Table 11 ‣ Physical boundary cases. ‣ 3.4 Closing the Recursive Loop ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
collects the systems that describe themselves as recursive
self-improvement.

### 3.1 Improving Policies, World Models, and Knowledge

This section reviews the base loop of physical self-improvement:
experience improves what the robot does, and the data, models, and
skills it leaves behind can help later learners. These are the first two
claims of
Section [2.2](#S2.SS2 "2.2 Defining Recursive Self-Improvement ‣ 2 Foundations of Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI"),
behavioral improvement and later-learning benefit. We follow the change
to where it is kept, in a policy
(Section [3.1.1](#S3.SS1.SSS1 "3.1.1 Policy Updates ‣ 3.1 Improving Policies, World Models, and Knowledge ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")),
a world model
(Section [3.1.2](#S3.SS1.SSS2 "3.1.2 World Models for Prediction and Practice ‣ 3.1 Improving Policies, World Models, and Knowledge ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")),
or memories, skills, and code
(Section [3.1.3](#S3.SS1.SSS3 "3.1.3 Memories, Skills, Code, and Runtimes ‣ 3.1 Improving Policies, World Models, and Knowledge ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")).
The learning procedure that produces these changes stays fixed here;
where a study also changes how experience is collected, judged, or
turned into updates, that part appears in
Section [3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Improving Learning Procedures ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI").

#### 3.1.1 Policy Updates

The most direct way for experience to help is to change the policy
itself, and on the path to RSI the policy is also the most common target
of a revised learning procedure. A deployed policy determines both what
the robot does and which situations later appear in its training data,
so the question to ask of new data is what learning signal they contain.
Four kinds of signal recur. _Relabeling_ reinterprets behavior that has
already happened: an attempt that pushed the cup aside instead of
grasping it is still a correct example of how to push the cup aside. A
_reward_ scores attempted outcomes so that optimization can prefer
better ones. A _correction_ supplies an action that the policy did not
take, typically from a person who intervenes. _Replay_ reuses earlier
experience to preserve or recover previously learned behavior
(Figure [5](#S3.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 3.1.1 Policy Updates ‣ 3.1 Improving Policies, World Models, and Knowledge ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")).
Each signal fits a different failure.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 5: Four teaching signals from physical experience. Each column
follows the grasp example: what was experienced, what the signal changes
in the training data, and representative systems from this section.

##### From practice to training targets.

A recorded trajectory becomes useful for learning only once a goal,
reward, or action label is attached to it. Hindsight experience
replay ([Andrychowicz et al., 2017](#bib.bib10)) relabels an attempt
with the goal it actually achieved, and SOAR ([Zhou et al.,
2025c](#bib.bib374)) carries this achieved-goal relabeling to
goal-conditioned imitation. Earlier large-scale systems such as
MT-Opt ([Kalashnikov et al., 2022](#bib.bib122)) shared physical
outcomes across twelve tasks; pretrained generalists change the starting
point, because practice can refine behavior that is already useful, and
value-based fine-tuning must then keep offline estimates calibrated, as
Cal-QL ([Nakamoto et al., 2023](#bib.bib204)) does in simulation.
RoboCat ([Bousmalis et al., 2024](#bib.bib28)) closes the resulting
cycle: a generalist adapted to a target task from demonstrations
collects trajectories that, mixed with retained multi-task data, retrain
the generalist offline. RoboCat also relabels unsuccessful episodes with
the goals they reached, whereas SOAR retrains only on attempts that its
fixed VLM judges successful
(Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Reported Outcomes and Experimental Context ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")).

Adding more of the robot’s own data does not necessarily improve the
targets it learns from. In their study of mostly single-task policies on
five simulated and two real manipulation tasks, [Mirchandani et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib199) find that added autonomous data yield modest gains
that saturate and, over two to four collection rounds, can regress. On
two of the tasks, human demonstrations started from conditions where
rollouts had failed help more than randomly chosen ones, whereas
autonomous collection from the same conditions offers no comparable
advantage. More state diversity in demonstration data does not always
help, whereas inconsistent actions often hurt ([Belkhale et al.,
2023](#bib.bib23)). These results separate two needs, _finding_ the
difficult conditions and _supplying useful actions_ there; repeating the
policy’s familiar successes addresses neither.

##### From feedback to better actions.

Relabeling cannot supply an action the policy never produced, but an
incomplete attempt can still reveal partial progress, and a person can
replace part of it with a corrective motion. SI-EFM ([Ghasemipour
et al., 2025](#bib.bib84)) takes the first route: a frozen model of the
steps remaining to a goal rewards each step that brings the robot
closer, and policy gradients then learn from incomplete real-robot
attempts without new demonstrations, though only among variations that
the policy actually tries. FAR ([Hao et al., 2026](#bib.bib96)) uses
failed attempts in a different way: it turns them into preference data
that steers retries away from the failed behavior and adds successful
recoveries to later training, with gains in simulation and on real
manipulation tasks.

Corrections take the second route. HIL-SERL ([Luo et al.,
2025](#bib.bib184)) builds on SERL ([Luo et al., 2024](#bib.bib183)),
which combines off-policy learning, learned reward classifiers, and
reset policies, and adds online human interventions so that corrective
transitions inform the critic that guides the actor. RECAP ([Physical
Intelligence et al., 2026](#bib.bib224)) conditions the policy on the
advantage of each action, fitted from deployment trajectories and expert
corrections. Max-Q selective imitation ([Wang and Wang,
2026](#bib.bib296)) regresses the actor toward whichever action a Monte
Carlo chunk critic scores higher: its own action or a replay-buffer
action, which is often an intervention. The target therefore shifts from
corrections to the policy’s own behavior as it improves. On real USB
insertion, it reaches 99% success after half an hour, whereas HIL-SERL
needs about five hours to reach its 100% ceiling (each at its best
checkpoint). SiLRI ([Zhao et al., 2025](#bib.bib366)) treats human
interventions as possibly suboptimal: it poses real-world RL as a
constrained problem whose bound at each state is set by the uncertainty
of the interventions, solved with a state-wise Lagrange multiplier, and
reaches 90% success on real manipulation tasks in at most half the time
HIL-SERL needs. The same recorded transition can become a value target,
a weighted action target, or a conditioning variable, as RAPolicy ([Yang
et al., 2026a](#bib.bib325)), SI-EFM, and RECAP illustrate, and which of
these the learner receives changes what it learns.

Two studies keep a pretrained VLA frozen during online learning and
train an added module alongside it. BEE ([Zhao et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib364)) uses the consistency of human corrections to
constrain RL updates to a residual policy around a frozen VLA. On three
real tasks and one simulated task, it reaches 91.2% average success
against 57.5% for an RL baseline at a matched online-data budget. RL
Token ([Xu et al., 2026b](#bib.bib317)) instead adapts a VLA to expose a
compact readout, keeps it frozen, and trains a small actor–critic on
that readout online. On four real tasks, minutes to a few hours of
practice speed up the hardest phase by up to 3$`\times`$ and raise
success as judged by a human operator, for example from 20% to 65% on
screw installation. Outside manipulation, SELFI ([Hirose et al.,
2024](#bib.bib100)) fine-tunes a pretrained navigation policy with
online model-free RL whose Q-values keep the model-based objective of
its offline pretraining, improving collision avoidance and, in a user
study, social compliance in real environments.

Reward-guided post-training of VLAs has scaled mainly in simulation,
while its most reliable results come from smaller hardware studies.
VLA-RL ([Lu et al., 2025](#bib.bib179)) on LIBERO ([Liu et al.,
2023a](#bib.bib164)) and $`\pi_{\texttt{RL}}`$ ([Chen et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib40)) run in simulation, and FLaRe ([Hu et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib108)) and SimpleVLA-RL ([Li et al., 2026c](#bib.bib147))
add real-robot results. In eight-task hardware studies, ConRFT ([Chen
et al., 2025d](#bib.bib48)) reaches 96.3% average success after 45–90
minutes of online fine-tuning and RL-100 ([Lei et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib141)) succeeds in 1,000 of 1,000 evaluation episodes.
Task-specific hardware studies such as GR-RL ([Li et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib154)) for shoe lacing and VLA-Precision ([Su et al.,
2026](#bib.bib253)) for chemistry tasks push precision further
(Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Reported Outcomes and Experimental Context ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")).
Autonomous real-world RL also reaches beyond tabletop arms: on Spot
mobile manipulators, task-relevant autonomy, behavior priors, and
generic rewards reach 80% average success on four tasks ([Mendonca
et al., 2024](#bib.bib195)).

Without per-task success checks, such training needs rewards that
generalize, and the stricter test of a learned reward is the behavior it
teaches rather than its prediction accuracy. Pretrained vision and
language models supply them as zero-shot similarities in
VLM-RM ([Rocamonde et al., 2024](#bib.bib235)) and RoboCLIP ([Sontakke
et al., 2023](#bib.bib251)), both evaluated in simulation, or as
embedding distances learned from human video in VIP ([Ma et al.,
2023b](#bib.bib189)) and LIV ([Ma et al., 2023a](#bib.bib188)), both
with real-robot evaluations. ReWiND ([Zhang et al.,
2025c](#bib.bib353)), RoboReward ([Lee et al., 2026b](#bib.bib140)), and
VLAC ([Zhai et al., 2025](#bib.bib345)) judge learned rewards by how
they transfer and by the behavior they teach; VLAC raises real success
on four tasks from about 30% to 90% within 200 episodes. Finer progress
distinctions preserve more of what incomplete attempts teach:
SARM2 ([Chen et al., 2026e](#bib.bib42)) conditions its reward model on
the estimated task stage, adapts it once, and holds it fixed while the
SPIRAL loop learns residual corrections to a frozen VLA. On crumpled
garments, three SPIRAL rounds raise success from 4/12 to 8/12, while the
matched loop with only a sparse success reward falls from 4/12 to 2/12.

##### From proposals to policies.

Feedback that can rank behavior leaves a second choice: where the
improvement should live. Choosing among proposals can improve execution
without retraining, as V-GPS ([Nakamoto et al., 2024](#bib.bib205)) does
by reranking a frozen policy’s proposals with an offline value function;
PA-RL ([Mark et al., 2024](#bib.bib192)) also improves sampled actions
under a critic and trains the policy on them with a supervised loss.
Learned judges can steer a frozen policy in the same way.
UF-OPS ([Attarian et al., 2026](#bib.bib16)) trains success and
time-to-success verifiers once on the policy’s labeled rollouts and
selects among sampled action chunks at run time, with reported gains of
25 to 80 percentage points on five real Aloha tasks. World-Coherent
Decoding ([Zhang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib348)) learns during deployment
to rank a frozen world action model’s sampled futures by the mismatch
between predicted and observed frames. In RoboTwin 2.0 simulation, under
the authors’ limited-randomization protocol, it raises Hard-split
success from 55.80% to 60.90%. Keeping scoring, improvement, and policy
change separate avoids the need to adapt policy gradients to each action
representation, whether iteratively denoised chunks in Diffusion
Policy ([Chi et al., 2023](#bib.bib52)), discretized tokens in
OpenVLA ([Kim et al., 2024](#bib.bib127)), or flow matching in
$`\pi_{0}`$ ([Black et al., 2025](#bib.bib25)). Selection gains can stay
in the selector or be absorbed into the generator. VERITAS ([Zhang and
Shah, 2026](#bib.bib357)) behavior-clones trajectories steered toward
agreement with a visual path proposed by a VLM. Q-Planning ([Giridhar
et al., 2026](#bib.bib86)) instead leaves the cloned policy unchanged
and updates a Q-function from successful and failed rollouts. On its two
real-robot tasks, terminal rewards come from human episode labels and
success is measured on the collection episodes themselves.

Both routes stay bounded by their proposals: if the generator never
produces a grasp that avoids the slip, no selector can recover one. A
_residual_ policy modifies the proposed motion while keeping the base
policy as a prior. ResiP ([Ankile et al., 2025](#bib.bib11)) trains one
in simulation and then distills it into a vision policy co-trained with
real demonstrations. DSRL ([Wagenmaker et al., 2025](#bib.bib272))
instead steers the input noise of a frozen diffusion policy, searching
only within its learned distribution. DPPO ([Ren et al.,
2025](#bib.bib231)) fine-tunes the diffusion policy itself and transfers
a simulation-trained assembly policy to hardware. Expanding proposals
helps only if the resulting experience teaches the policy where it needs
help, which PLD ([Xiao et al., 2026a](#bib.bib305)) tests directly. A
residual-RL specialist takes over after the generalist has run for a
sampled number of steps, and the hybrid trajectories are distilled back.
In real cube pickup, a PLD specialist and an RLPD ([Ball et al.,
2023](#bib.bib19)) specialist both reach full success within two hours
from the same initialization, and each supplies 200 successful
trajectories to the same distillation. The resulting generalists
nevertheless differ, succeeding in 30 and 16 of 30 trials, respectively,
because only the PLD data include recoveries from the corner states that
the learner itself visits; collector success alone therefore does not
reveal training value. Delay creates a further mismatch: Real-Time
EXPO-FT ([Dong et al., 2026](#bib.bib64)) edits the action chunks of a
slower VLA with the latest observation and selects among candidates with
a critic, because an action can become wrong between prediction and
execution. Selection suffices when useful behavior already lies in the
proposal set; otherwise the generator must be optimized, corrected,
steered, or fine-tuned, and distillation retains corrections that should
become habitual
(Table [6](#S3.T6 "Table 6 ‣ From proposals to policies. ‣ 3.1.1 Policy Updates ‣ 3.1 Improving Policies, World Models, and Knowledge ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")).

##### From single runs to lifelong practice.

At scale, RoboNet ([Dasari et al., 2020](#bib.bib59)) pools trajectories
across laboratories and embodiments, and Learning While Deploying ([Wang
et al., 2026j](#bib.bib292)) repeatedly updates one generalist from
rollouts and interventions across sixteen robots. SOP ([Pan et al.,
2026](#bib.bib219)) streams on-policy experience and human interventions
from a fleet to a cloud learner and reports real-world performance that
scales near-linearly with the number of robots. OpenBot-Fleet ([Müller
et al., 2024](#bib.bib202)) sends learned navigation policies back to
user-operated robots. More sources widen coverage only where
observations, actions, and task definitions align. Practice also needs a
way back to a useful starting state: Leave No Trace ([Eysenbach et al.,
2018](#bib.bib73)) learns forward and reset policies in simulation,
ReLMM ([Sun et al., 2022](#bib.bib254)) learns reset-free on a physical
mobile manipulator, and MEDAL++ ([Sharma et al., 2023](#bib.bib243)) and
RoboFuME ([Yang et al., 2024a](#bib.bib327)) need only occasional manual
resets on real robots.

Against forgetting, capacity can be allocated or routed, as
AtomicVLA ([Zhang et al., 2026g](#bib.bib356)) grows expert modules for
atomic skills and CLARE ([Römer et al., 2026b](#bib.bib237)) expands and
selects adapters without task labels, or adaptation can be combined with
rehearsal, as in LifelongVLA ([He et al., 2026b](#bib.bib98)) and
iManip ([Zheng et al., 2025](#bib.bib368)), or with targeted replay, as
in Memory Anchors ([Du et al., 2026](#bib.bib65)). Separation costs
capacity and routing; retaining experience, as in gradient episodic
memory ([Lopez-Paz and Ranzato, 2017](#bib.bib176)), costs storage but
can also speed later tasks ([Xie and Finn, 2022](#bib.bib307)).
CIDER ([Li et al., 2026d](#bib.bib148)) freezes the accumulated policy
as a teacher before each new task and alternates current-task RL with
distillation on archived states; over six real tasks and three runs
each, the retained policy needs no more training steps to reach the
success criterion than the same RL agent from the common initialization,
and fewer on some tasks. Replay and distillation assume a fixed action
interface: FAN ([Hong et al., 2026a](#bib.bib101)) shows that updating
action-normalization statistics between tasks shifts the coordinates
shared by training and execution; statistics frozen after a small
task-independent calibration give the highest average score across four
real task streams.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

#### 3.1.2 World Models for Prediction and Practice

Physical trials are slow and costly, so a natural way to stretch them is
to learn a model of the world and practice inside it. A world model
predicts how a physical state may change after an action; for a grasp,
it might predict whether the object will stay between the fingers when
the gripper closes. The prediction can serve as a _plan_ that must be
translated into motion, as _imagined experience_ from which a policy is
trained, or as _predicted features_ supplied to a policy. Each role
tests a different form of _usability_: success in one role says little
about the others. Generative video models offer all three interfaces: a
generated video serves as a plan in UniPi ([Du et al.,
2023](#bib.bib66)), as a controllable simulator in UniSim ([Yang et al.,
2024b](#bib.bib330)) and, learned without action labels, in
Genie ([Bruce et al., 2024](#bib.bib31)), and as policy-training data in
DreamGen ([Jang et al., 2025](#bib.bib116)). Cosmos ([NVIDIA et al.,
2025](#bib.bib211)) develops world foundation models for physical
applications, WISA ([Wang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib280)) and PISA ([Li
et al., 2025a](#bib.bib145)) target physical consistency, and
SPIRAL ([Yang et al., 2026d](#bib.bib331)) (unrelated to the SPIRAL
policy loop of
Section [3.1.1](#S3.SS1.SSS1.Px2 "From feedback to better actions. ‣ 3.1.1 Policy Updates ‣ 3.1 Improving Policies, World Models, and Knowledge ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI"))
updates its generator with a critic that checks action adherence and
physical realism. A world model can also enter the learning procedure by
judging candidate policies or changes before they reach hardware
(Sections [3.2.2](#S3.SS2.SSS2 "3.2.2 Judging Outcomes ‣ 3.2 Improving Learning Procedures ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
and [4.4](#S4.SS4.SSS0.Px5 "Where recursion could start. ‣ 4.4 Making Improvement Recursive ‣ 4 Challenges and Future Directions for Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")).

##### Using models to plan and train.

Classical model-based methods supplied the main ingredients.
Dyna ([Sutton, 1990](#bib.bib256)) interleaves real and modeled
experience, PILCO ([Deisenroth and Rasmussen, 2011](#bib.bib60)) and
PETS ([Chua et al., 2018](#bib.bib54)) account for model uncertainty,
MBPO ([Janner et al., 2019](#bib.bib117)) keeps imagined rollouts short
to limit compounding error, self-supervised visual planning ([Ebert
et al., 2017](#bib.bib71)) plans through learned video prediction, and
latent world models ([Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018](#bib.bib91); [Hafner
et al., 2020](#bib.bib92)) train policies in compact dynamics, as
DayDreamer ([Wu et al., 2023](#bib.bib302)) did on physical robots. A
model’s value for control need not track its prediction
accuracy ([Lambert et al., 2020](#bib.bib135); [Farahmand et al.,
2017](#bib.bib75); [Grimm et al., 2020](#bib.bib88)).

Planning first exposes an interface problem: a predicted video of the
gripper closing is not yet a robot command. SILVR ([Luo et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib182)) translates video plans through a separately trained
inverse-dynamics model, and on hardware its successful executions update
only the task video planner. In its simulated Meta-World ([Yu et al.,
2019](#bib.bib338)) ablation over twelve unseen tasks, updating both
planner and translator reaches 44.2% success, against 26.8% with the
translator frozen: an improving planner can be held back by a translator
that cannot express its new motions. The hardware counterpart of this
comparison remains to be run.

A model used for training shifts the burden to policy optimization, and
its gain depends on how far the policy may optimize against the model.
RISE ([Yang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib326)) freezes its learned dynamics
and value models, limits imagined interactions to two steps, and updates
an advantage-conditioned VLA; its hardware comparison reimplements
RECAP ([Physical Intelligence et al., 2026](#bib.bib224)) with the same
$`\pi_{0.5}`$ ([Physical Intelligence et al., 2025](#bib.bib223))
initialization, because the $`\pi_{0.6}`$ model used by RECAP is not
available. PlayWorld ([Yin et al., 2026b](#bib.bib334)) trains only the
small DSRL ([Wagenmaker et al., 2025](#bib.bib272)) policy that chooses
its generator’s input noise against the fitted world model, rewarded by
a progress estimator trained on demonstrations; with twenty hardware
trials per checkpoint, its best reported task improves by 65 percentage
points over the base policy, yet later optimization inside the model can
reduce real success. WMPO ([Zhu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib377)),
Ctrl-World ([Guo et al., 2025](#bib.bib89)), ProphRL ([Zhang et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib352)), and World-Gymnast ([Sharma et al.,
2026](#bib.bib242)) likewise improve VLAs with imagined rollouts.
Fine-tuning on imagined successes raises Ctrl-World’s policy success by
44.7 percentage points, and ProphRL, which runs flow-policy GRPO inside
an action-conditioned video model pretrained on more than 31M
trajectories, raises overall success on four real UR30e tasks by 24.6 to
30.0 percentage points over the starting policies of three VLA backbones
(Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Reported Outcomes and Experimental Context ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")).
Whether new physical experience should also repair the practice model is
a further choice, one that changes what later updates learn from;
Section [3.2.3](#S3.SS2.SSS3 "3.2.3 Shaping Training Data ‣ 3.2 Improving Learning Procedures ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
follows VLAW’s loop of this kind.
Figure [6](#S3.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Using models to plan and train. ‣ 3.1.2 World Models for Prediction and Practice ‣ 3.1 Improving Policies, World Models, and Knowledge ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
separates these decisions, and
Table [7](#S3.T7 "Table 7 ‣ Using models to plan and train. ‣ 3.1.2 World Models for Prediction and Practice ‣ 3.1 Improving Policies, World Models, and Knowledge ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
records what the main model-assisted studies update, hold fixed, and
compare.
