##### Feeding models the right data.

Whether new rollouts can repair a model depends on what they cover for
the component that consumes them. A contact model needs partial
contacts, slips, and recoveries, not only successes: PlayWorld collects
such evidence through autonomous play, SILVR through task-directed
rollouts from its current planner, and Motus2 ([Bi et al.,
2026](#bib.bib24)) routes curated successes to action generation and
failed or suboptimal interactions to dynamics or value prediction,
freezing its video backbone and evaluator during later policy
optimization. When natural failures miss the needed corrections,
XPACE ([Wei et al., 2026a](#bib.bib297)) constructs them: its world
model renders deviations from expert demonstrations followed by
recoveries, and fine-tuning on a mixture containing 8% of these examples
yields hardware gains across three tasks evaluated with twenty trials
per method. A failed contact may be valuable for predicting
consequences, while only a validated recovery should supervise the
action policy.

Dynamics can also change. Roughly 100 seconds of real quadrotor flight
support online identification of a residual dynamics model and in-flight
policy updates ([Ren et al., 2026](#bib.bib232)); Variational Neural
Dynamics ([Xing et al., 2026](#bib.bib314)) instead infers which
recurring operating condition applies from recent interaction; and
Self-adapting Robotic Agents ([Domberg and Schildbach,
2026](#bib.bib63)) detect out-of-distribution events from prediction
residuals and trigger fine-tuning. D-World ([Wen and Wang,
2026](#bib.bib299)), which its authors describe as recursive
self-improvement, keeps an explicit digital twin that a frozen language
model revises after each executed action chunk and accepts a revision
only when replayed residuals do not grow; on a real dual-arm robot, one
revision reduced a rendered-depth residual from 22.4 to 1.5 mm. After
damage, [Bongard et al. (2006)](#bib.bib27) revise a model of the
robot’s body and search it for a new gait, Intelligent Trial and
Error ([Cully et al., 2015](#bib.bib58)) searches a precomputed
repertoire of behaviors, and GrBAL ([Nagabandi et al.,
2019](#bib.bib203)) adapts a meta-learned dynamics prior
(Section [2.3](#S2.SS3.SSS0.Px4 "Meta-learning. ‣ 2.3 Relating RSI to Robot Learning ‣ 2 Foundations of Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")).
Which route saves physical trials depends on what useful structure
survives the change.

##### Shaping what models predict.

For control, a representation must distinguish futures that imply
different actions, which pixel-accurate prediction neither guarantees
nor requires. Joint-embedding predictive architectures predict in
learned feature spaces and plan toward goals there, as
V-JEPA 2-AC ([Assran et al., 2025](#bib.bib14)) and DINO-WM ([Zhou
et al., 2025a](#bib.bib370)) do, and D-JEPA ([Liu et al.,
2026e](#bib.bib171)) aligns competing predicted futures with the
candidate that executes best. Physical properties must remain readable:
in PokeWorld ([Tan et al., 2026a](#bib.bib262)), predicting touch makes
stiffness decodable whereas merely supplying touch as an input does not,
and PSG-JEPA ([Yan et al., 2026](#bib.bib324)) adds proprioceptive
objectives where forward prediction alone omits such structure.
DreamerV3 ([Hafner et al., 2025](#bib.bib93)), which reconstructs
observations, and TD-MPC2 ([Hansen et al., 2024](#bib.bib95)), which
does not, bracket the design space. Retrieved history in
Mem-World ([Zheng et al., 2026b](#bib.bib369)), force–torque prediction
in MuSe ([Clark et al., 2026](#bib.bib55)), and predicted fingertip
wrenches in TORL-VLA ([Zheng et al., 2026a](#bib.bib367)) supply
distinctions that camera data alone can miss.

The information must also reach the policy through a usable interface,
and the model must respond correctly to commands.
GigaBrain-0.5M\* ([GigaBrain Team et al., 2026](#bib.bib85)) conditions
action learning on predicted future-state tokens, whereas VLAW turns
predicted futures into reward-filtered training data; a conditioned
policy may ignore or over-rely on auxiliary tokens, whereas synthetic
data may amplify prediction errors. WorldEcho ([Chen et al.,
2026f](#bib.bib43)) shows that models trained only on expert
trajectories, given commands outside that distribution, either ignore
the commanded motion or produce visually invalid rollouts, and
CausalWorld ([Ahmed et al., 2021](#bib.bib3)) lets physical and visual
variables be changed independently. Across embodiments, particle-based
action representations ([He et al., 2026c](#bib.bib99)) offer a shared
geometric interface, while XEWorld ([Chen et al., 2026i](#bib.bib47))
finds that current models bind joint commands more readily to familiar
appearance than to transferable kinematics. A visually plausible model
may still lack decision-relevant state, a usable interface, or correct
responses to intervention.

##### Judging models by their use.

Failure can enter at four links between a model and its policy:
transition prediction, outcome scoring, policy optimization, or
translation into executable motion. End-to-end hardware results, as in
RISE and PlayWorld, measure joint usefulness but do not say which link
broke, so evaluation needs both final performance and comparisons that
change one link at a time. DexTouch-WM ([Qin et al., 2026](#bib.bib227))
shows why. Its world model trained on mixed human and robot data
improves held-out prediction and, on average, agreement between policy
rankings in imagination and on hardware, yet replacing 100 of 200 real
training trajectories with synthetic counterparts generated by this
model lowers the mean physical partial-credit score for each of three
policy families (FTP-1, $`\pi_{0.5}`$, and X-VLA) across four tasks. A
model can become a better surrogate evaluator and still produce a worse
training mixture.

Other methods change how predictions are consumed. WISE ([Zhang et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib347)) calls a frozen world model only at states where
interaction matters and bounds the imagined horizon, and HaWMPO ([Chen
et al., 2026j](#bib.bib49)) trains a hallucination estimator on
discrepancies between generated and observed outcomes and uses it to
soften rewards from unreliable action chunks. How prediction is queried
also matters: in CaliBench ([Sadeghi et al., 2026](#bib.bib239)),
individually plausible videos can have poorly calibrated outcome
frequencies, and in a simulated differential-drive study ([Raghavan and
Singh, 2026](#bib.bib229)), a 20-step rollout without intermediate
measurements picks a different state estimator than closed-loop tracking
in 18 of 24 sensing conditions, whereas replay error under the recorded
schedule disagrees in five. Evaluation should reproduce the actions,
horizon, and observation schedule of the policy’s use.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

#### 3.1.3 Memories, Skills, Code, and Runtimes

Not every useful change needs to enter a policy’s weights or a world
model. A robot that misses grasps might remember that a particular
object tends to slip, save a regrasp routine that worked, or add a
monitor that interrupts the policy when slip is detected. We use
_memory_ for stored information that must be interpreted when it is
used, _skill_ for a callable behavior with an execution interface, and
_runtime_ or _software_ for the logic that retrieves, composes,
monitors, or repairs those behaviors
(Figure [7](#S3.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ 3.1.3 Memories, Skills, Code, and Runtimes ‣ 3.1 Improving Policies, World Models, and Knowledge ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")).
The same artifact can cross these boundaries (a recovery written down as
text becomes a skill once a controller can execute it), but the
distinction identifies who uses the change next; for all three, the
question is whether a change kept outside model weights is _usable_. On
the path to RSI, external knowledge is also where a system can keep the
repair knowledge that recursion requires
(Section [2.2](#S2.SS2 "2.2 Defining Recursive Self-Improvement ‣ 2 Foundations of Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")).

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 7: Three forms of external knowledge in the grasp example. Each
panel shows one saved form of the slip repair and representative systems
from this section; reuse on another robot first checks the interface.

Earlier systems kept different kinds of artifacts. Options ([Sutton
et al., 1999](#bib.bib258)) encode temporally extended behaviors that a
higher-level controller can call, and Horde ([Sutton et al.,
2011](#bib.bib259)) learns many sensorimotor predictions in parallel.
RoboEarth ([Waibel et al., 2011](#bib.bib273)) shares models and action
recipes among robots. Code as Policies ([Liang et al.,
2023](#bib.bib159)) writes programs against perception and control APIs,
and Inner Monologue ([Huang et al., 2023](#bib.bib111)) feeds execution
feedback back into planning. In digital environments, including
games ([Luo et al., 2026b](#bib.bib185)), Voyager ([Wang et al.,
2024a](#bib.bib277)) accumulates executable skills and Reflexion ([Shinn
et al., 2023](#bib.bib245)) stores written reflections on earlier
failures, showing how a frozen model can still take part in an agent
that improves; the _Weights or Skills?_ survey ([Jena et al.,
2026](#bib.bib118)) reviews this broader choice. Physical reuse
additionally needs valid sensing, control, and conditions of
applicability.

##### Remembering experience.

Memory systems differ in what they store, how strongly they abstract it,
through which interface it is read, and how long it persists, and a
memory helps only if these choices preserve a relation that a later
decision can exploit. Some systems keep the scene and past interaction
themselves: RoboMemory ([Lei et al., 2025b](#bib.bib142)) and
AllDayNav ([Yin et al., 2026a](#bib.bib333)) preserve continuity of the
environment and of past interaction, and PhyAgentOS ([Liu et al.,
2026h](#bib.bib174)) keeps sessions, evidence, recovered lessons, and
capability descriptions as versioned records inside a runtime that also
checks compatibility, supervises execution, and invokes recovery, so its
gains belong to the integrated package.

Others distill experience into reusable guidance, which must then be
checked against later conditions. Robo-Cortex ([Chan et al.,
2026](#bib.bib35)) distills progress and failure histories into
principles and induced navigation heuristics, evaluated mainly in unseen
settings of the Habitat simulator ([Savva et al., 2019](#bib.bib240))
with a preliminary physical study of ten navigation goals.
RoboHarn-Evo ([Bao et al., 2026](#bib.bib20)) also revises what it
stores: physical feedback updates task- and action-level entries
together with their stated applicability, and knowledge acquired in
simulation reaches 41.7% mean zero-shot success on real tasks, rising to
62.5% after updates from real interaction. PhysMem ([Li et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib146)) makes the check explicit: a frozen VLM planner
commits a hypothesis about physical properties to memory only after
targeted interaction verifies it. On simulated medium-difficulty brick
insertion this reaches 76% success against 53% without memory and 23%
when raw experience is retrieved directly (100 episodes per condition,
three seeds), so retrieving raw experience can do worse than having no
memory; its real xArm6 experiments report plan quality over 30-minute
deployment sessions. PragmaBot ([Qu et al., 2025](#bib.bib228))
summarizes the successful episodes of a real legged manipulator into a
retrievable memory, raising single-trial success over twelve scenarios,
eight of them new but structurally similar, from 22% for a planner
without memory to 80%. Storage is only half of reuse: a retriever must
select the record, and a recipient must assign it the right role.

How long a memory lives also limits what it can show. With the
foundation policy of Zeva ([Chen et al., 2026a](#bib.bib37)) fixed,
removing its interaction memory lowers success by 10–20 percentage
points on five real ChemLab-Evo tasks, but the store is cleared before
each episode, so the benefit is adaptation across retries within an
episode.

##### Reusing skills and code.

A one-off recovery becomes a reusable skill only when it is detached
from the incident that produced it, with an implementation, a callable
interface, and stated conditions and effects that let a planner place it
in a new sequence. Implementations come from demonstrations in
LOTUS ([Wan et al., 2024](#bib.bib274)) and Uni-Skill ([Xie et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib310)), and from a person when the library cannot carry
out the plan in HaLP ([Parakh et al., 2024](#bib.bib220)). The robot’s
own execution supplies them in MobiAgent ([Liu et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib165)) and ReSYNC ([Li et al., 2026a](#bib.bib144)).
MobiAgent clusters verified deployment rollouts into atomic skills and
raises real success on an Astribot S1 from 32.5% to 57.5%, and ReSYNC
learns recovery policies together with the symbolic predicates and
operators that let a planner compose them.

Code-writing agents often call two artifacts “skills”: a callable
routine and guidance for constructing one. LRLL ([Tziafas and Kasaei,
2024](#bib.bib271)) distills simulated instruction–program pairs into
callable Python APIs under a curriculum. ASPIRE ([Lu et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib180)) retrieves guidance distilled from earlier program
repairs when debugging a new controller; on three physical tasks whose
embodiment and API differ from the simulation source, retrieval reduces
the reasoning tokens spent on the real robot, and held-out success is
unchanged on one task and improves on two. Reconstruct, Practice, Go
Real ([Wang et al., 2026i](#bib.bib291)) revises symbolic skills and its
system prompt during simulated practice, keeps a change only after a
cross-task check, and reaches 95.0% against 75.5% for ASPIRE on held-out
initializations of 22 simulated tasks; the frozen system succeeds in all
30 physical trials.

Libraries can also be built in advance and frozen, and the clearest
results come from passing a frozen library to fresh or weaker agents.
RATs ([Zhang et al., 2026f](#bib.bib355)) distills successful play into
a code-skill library for simulated LIBERO-PRO tasks. EmbodiedEvo ([Li
et al., 2026g](#bib.bib151)) keeps code skills and written lessons that
raise fresh agents’ success on unseen layouts of the RoboDojo simulation
benchmark ([Chen et al., 2026g](#bib.bib45)) from 8.50% to 30.17%, with
similar success at 53.0% lower execution cost than the raw interaction
history. Its frozen library also raises a weaker executor that failed to
acquire it by 8.86 percentage points over no experience.
PhysRSI-eval ([Li et al., 2026j](#bib.bib156)) freezes GPT-6 Astra
workspaces after six rounds of revision on six RoboDojo tasks and tests
each on five unseen layouts with no further revision; across 12
workspaces, the stored files alone succeed in 25 of 60 tests. Workspaces
pooled from the other tasks also bring the first success earlier in
three cases, for example from round 14 to round 7 for Claude Opus 5.5 on
the Organize Table task. RoboSkill ([Xie et al., 2026c](#bib.bib311))
reports real-robot gains on its hard tasks, and Agent as Policy ([Jia
et al., 2026](#bib.bib119)) shortens execution across repeated real
trials. Embodied Turing Machines ([Hu et al., 2026b](#bib.bib109)) make
every decision in code on simulated bimanual tasks
(Table [11](#S3.T11 "Table 11 ‣ Physical boundary cases. ‣ 3.4 Closing the Recursive Loop ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")).
A frozen library can also be written from demonstrations rather than
practice. In an evaluation of GPT-6-Astra ([Cai et al.,
2026](#bib.bib34)), the model studies a task’s training demonstrations
and writes task guidance, motion references, executable helpers, and
recovery procedures into a package that is frozen before testing and
given to every fresh test session. On four simulated humanoid tasks of
the SIMPLE benchmark, the package raises success from 70.8% to 90.8%
(120 episodes per condition), with gains that depend on how closely the
demonstrations cover the test tasks.

Studies that vary the retained artifact while holding its user fixed
show most clearly what the artifact must encode. ReTrace ([Yu et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib340)) lets a model controlling a real Franka arm trace a
late failure to an earlier decision, test one correction per attempt,
and keep supported corrections as a text skill. With skills that one
model learned in a few attempts, a second executing model raises plug
insertion and ball pouring from 0% to 80% and 100%, respectively, over
ten real trials each. In a code-transfer study ([Kuroki and Tang,
2026](#bib.bib133)), with the coding model, cases, interfaces, and
per-session limits held fixed, mean success on nine new tasks in the
simulated RoboCasa environment ([Nasiriany et al., 2024](#bib.bib206))
is 45.2% without references, 41.5% with initial source programs, and
57.0% with execution-optimized ones: a retained artifact helps only if
it encodes distinctions that the next synthesizer can exploit.
Table [8](#S3.T8 "Table 8 ‣ Reusing skills and code. ‣ 3.1.3 Memories, Skills, Code, and Runtimes ‣ 3.1 Improving Policies, World Models, and Knowledge ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
summarizes selected external-artifact updates of this section and their
outcome checks.

[TABLE]

Table 8: External-knowledge updates.

Even a correct skill fails if it is called under the wrong conditions,
and some systems revise those conditions directly. VASO ([Yang et al.,
2026e](#bib.bib332)) model-checks skill-based plans against
temporal-logic specifications and turns counterexample traces into
updates of each skill’s semantic contract. Across tasks for a Jackal
ground robot and the PX4 autopilot, eleven specifications, and 400
generated plans, the optimized skills reach 97.2% (handcrafted
alignment) or 96.8% (automatic) specification compliance; compliance
holds relative to the encoded propositions, and unmodeled sensing or
contact errors lie outside it. The conditions can also concern the robot
itself. KnowBody ([Lou et al., 2026](#bib.bib177)) keeps an explicit,
revisable model of how the robot’s body produces effects, with the VLM
frozen, and rechecks knowledge that depends on a revised body estimate
before reusing it. Over 32 fixed-budget trials on four real-robot tasks,
it completes 75% against 25% for the native harness. With persistent
updates, its planner rounds fall by 29–53% from the first to the fifth
recorded success. Composition also creates handoffs, as when a placed
mug hides the next object from the camera, so a skill’s stated effects
should include the state it hands to its successor.

##### Revising the runtime.

The runtime selects context, monitors progress, interrupts, routes
control to recoveries, and decides when the nominal policy may resume;
revising it can change the effective agent while the weights of planner
and controller stay fixed. The reported comparisons show that runtime
components interact, and most of them are measured in simulation.
SHAPER ([Wang et al., 2026e](#bib.bib285)) edits textual procedural
guidance and a Python harness around a frozen planner and executor, and
on VLABench ([Zhang et al., 2025d](#bib.bib358)) the two edits are not
additive: the full configuration scores 34.50% against 28.25% for the
seed, less than the skill-only and harness-only gains combined.
Zetta ([Ding et al., 2026](#bib.bib62)) grows code-based critics that
detect local failure signatures such as a slipping grasp and promotes a
critic–recovery patch only after diagnostic replay and a fresh
closed-loop rollout. Harness VLA ([Zhang et al., 2026j](#bib.bib361))
keeps a VLA frozen as a retryable contact primitive and learns from
execution traces when it and a few analytic primitives apply. SHAPER and
Zetta are evaluated in simulation; Harness VLA measures its gains in
simulation, with demonstrations on two dual-arm Franka setups.
Baton ([Xu et al., 2026a](#bib.bib316)) explores each subtask separately
around a frozen VLA and stores memories of the transitions between
subtasks; with exploration on one scene seed and evaluation on ten
held-out seeds of 26 simulated RoboMemArena tasks, it reaches 63.5% task
success against 46.1% for the strongest prior method, and the system is
also run on a real PiPER-X arm.

Several systems revise programs and tools around a frozen model and gate
what they admit. DynaHarness ([Deng et al., 2026](#bib.bib61)) admits a
revision of the capabilities around a frozen $`\pi_{0.5}`$ only after
paired regression checks, and its frozen final system reaches 75.2% on
800 newly sampled simulated LIBERO-PRO initial states against 17.5% for
the bare policy. HarnessPAI ([Wang et al., 2026g](#bib.bib289)),
evaluated only in simulation, has a coding agent revise a task program
around a frozen action model and reaches 96.5% on simulated LIBERO-PRO
tasks, on evaluation seeds that include its development seeds;
fine-tuning $`\pi_{0.5}`$ on the harness’s successful rollouts raises
held-out-seed success from 34.9% to 73.7%. URAI ([Ge et al.,
2026](#bib.bib83)) has a frozen agent call validated tools one complete
motion at a time, raising pooled success on simulated RoboDojo tasks
from 18.0% under direct fingertip control to 53.0%; tool revision by its
programming agent appears in an author-steered case study. RoboRSI ([Wen
et al., 2026](#bib.bib300)), named for recursive self-improvement,
confines each patch to the skill branch where a failure began and
releases it only after review, tests, and replay; on three of its four
simulation benchmarks, its gains are measured while it improves online
on the evaluation tasks
(Table [11](#S3.T11 "Table 11 ‣ Physical boundary cases. ‣ 3.4 Closing the Recursive Loop ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")).
RACaP ([Li et al., 2026k](#bib.bib157)) replaces its parent system only
when a candidate achieves strictly higher success under identical tasks,
seeds, and budgets: over 596 simulated development episodes, nine of the
23 tested candidates were promoted, and the frozen result reaches 54.4%
on the 90 LIBERO tasks it evolved on and 45.0% zero-shot on LIBERO-PRO.
In DynaHarness, HarnessPAI, URAI, and RoboRSI, any agent that writes
revisions is a fixed model, although HarnessPAI’s growing library of
failure-to-repair notes changes what its program writer knows.

A different route trains the program writer itself. PyRUA-Lean ([Si
et al., 2026](#bib.bib247)) fine-tunes a 4B model that composes robot
primitives, including VLA policies, into Python cells on 45 simulated
LIBERO-PRO task instances, raising its success on unseen instances from
18.8% to 44.1%.

##### Transferring across robots.

Moving knowledge to another robot can fail at each level of description.
Saved as a task, the regrasp transfers only if the receiving robot can
ground it in skills of its own, and saved as a named skill, it transfers
only if that robot implements the same effect. Saved as an end-effector
motion, it transfers only if both robots interpret the motion alike;
saved as joint commands, it transfers only to an arm of the same kind.
SayCan ([Ichter et al., 2023](#bib.bib114)) grounds skills by combining
their usefulness for the task with their estimated chance of success,
while Open X-Embodiment ([Open X-Embodiment Collaboration et al.,
2024](#bib.bib215)) standardizes data from twenty-two embodiments but
maps actions to a coarse common end-effector format that leaves
coordinate frames unaligned, so the same numerical action can induce
different motions on different robots. RoboFoundry ([Liang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib161)) separates embodiment-invariant decisions from
embodiment-specific execution so that evolved memories and recovery
skills can transfer, and PhyAgentOS checks observations, action
semantics, timing, capabilities, and safety configuration before
building adapters; its validation on Franka, PIPER, and Dobot arms tests
whether the interface carries over, not whether a saved lesson does.
ASPIRE tests a lesson on a single receiving robot: guidance from
simulated Franka repairs helps a coding agent debug programs for a
bimanual robot with a different API, on which no simulated program runs
unchanged. SHAPER, Zetta, and the code-transfer study move artifacts
across simulated tasks but not across robots. Evaluation should hold the
artifact or the adapter fixed while varying the other.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### 3.2 Improving Learning Procedures

The changes reviewed so far also alter what the next round of learning
starts from. An improved policy reaches states that were previously
inaccessible, so the data available for the next update change too. The
resulting experience can expose distinctions missing from supervision;
revised supervision changes what an update teaches; and the repair that
follows can become evidence for constructing later updates. Along this
chain, a change of any form can take on a new role in the _learning
procedure_
(Figure [4](#S2.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Where experience leaves a change. ‣ 2.2 Defining Recursive Self-Improvement ‣ 2 Foundations of Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")).
Improving that procedure is where RSI would begin, because it changes
how the robot learns rather than only what it does.

Reuse and procedure change can overlap, but they answer different
questions: reuse asks whether a change is carried forward, whereas
procedure change asks whether it alters collection, judgment, or
updating for a later learner. We take the procedure’s decisions in turn:
where the next experience comes from ($`c`$,
Section [3.2.1](#S3.SS2.SSS1 "3.2.1 Choosing What to Practice ‣ 3.2 Improving Learning Procedures ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")),
how outcomes are judged ($`e`$,
Section [3.2.2](#S3.SS2.SSS2 "3.2.2 Judging Outcomes ‣ 3.2 Improving Learning Procedures ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")),
what an update learns from ($`d`$,
Section [3.2.3](#S3.SS2.SSS3 "3.2.3 Shaping Training Data ‣ 3.2 Improving Learning Procedures ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")),
and how the update is made ($`u`$,
Section [3.2.4](#S3.SS2.SSS4 "3.2.4 Constructing Updates ‣ 3.2 Improving Learning Procedures ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")).
Section [3.2.5](#S3.SS2.SSS5 "3.2.5 Automating Experiments ‣ 3.2 Improving Learning Procedures ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
then turns to how whole experimental loops are run, which can change
several of these decisions at once, and
Table [10](#S3.T10 "Table 10 ‣ 3.2.5 Automating Experiments ‣ 3.2 Improving Learning Procedures ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
summarizes representative systems. A changed procedure is not yet an
improved one: improvement requires that a learner guided by the revised
procedure learn better than a matched learner guided by the earlier one
(Section [2.2](#S2.SS2 "2.2 Defining Recursive Self-Improvement ‣ 2 Foundations of Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI");
Figure [8](#S3.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ 3.2 Improving Learning Procedures ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")).

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 8: Does a revised component help the next learner? Two matched
learners differ only in the component under test, here an evaluator.
Their common outcome check stays fixed and separate from that evaluator;
comparing the learners’ outcomes tests procedure improvement.

#### 3.2.1 Choosing What to Practice

Once a recovery removes a coarse grasp failure, the remaining errors may
concentrate on subtle contact events. More demonstrations of the old
kind may then be less useful than tactile checks, a finer reward, or a
new rule for editing skills. Better execution has changed the learning
problem, and the system now has to find the experience that teaches what
is still missing. The most useful experience for an improved policy need
not come from the distribution that served its predecessor, and choosing
it involves three decisions: which tasks or states to practice, what
supervision an attempt needs, and when collection is safe. Active
learning ([Cohn et al., 1996](#bib.bib56)) selects observations for
their expected contribution to learning; in robotics, however, selecting
an observation often means choosing a behavior, task, environment, or
trajectory that must actually be executed. SAC-X ([Riedmiller et al.,
2018](#bib.bib233)) schedules auxiliary behaviors that help the robot
reach sparse rewards; automatic domain randomization ([OpenAI et al.,
2019](#bib.bib216)) widens the range of simulated conditions as the
policy becomes competent; and Enhanced POET ([Wang et al.,
2020](#bib.bib286)) co-evolves environments together with the policies
that solve them. In each case, what the learner can already do helps
determine what it encounters next.

At the task level, the frontier worth targeting is learnable challenge:
tasks hard enough to teach something and easy enough to be learned.
Methods based on intrinsic motivation ([Oudeyer et al.,
2007](#bib.bib218)), automatic curriculum learning ([Portelas et al.,
2020](#bib.bib226)), and autotelic agents that set their own
goals ([Colas et al., 2022](#bib.bib57)) track learning progress across
goals or environment parameters. Systems built on language models
enlarge the space of candidate lessons by generating tasks and
environments, as in GenSim ([Wang et al., 2024b](#bib.bib282)) and
RoboGen ([Wang et al., 2024d](#bib.bib294)); OMNI ([Zhang et al.,
2024](#bib.bib349)) combines estimated learning progress with a model of
what humans find interesting, while Eurekaverse ([Liang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib162)) generates environments that become progressively
more challenging while remaining diverse and learnable. AutoRT ([Ahn
et al., 2024](#bib.bib4)) proposes tasks with language models, filters
them against a written robot constitution, and over seven months
collected about 77,000 episodes on 53 robots. Generation supplies
possibilities, but a signal that depends on the learner’s current
capability is still needed to decide which possibility should become the
next lesson.

FIND ([Fang et al., 2026](#bib.bib74)) supplies such a signal on
hardware: a VLM agent selects feasible tasks with low recent success and
judges each attempt by comparing observations before and after
execution, and residual RL on a frozen $`\pi_{0.5}`$ raises success on
eight real tasks from 55% to 71.9%, while people still reset scenes when
needed. InSight ([Wang et al., 2026c](#bib.bib283)) lets a VLM name the
primitives a steerable VLA lacks for a new task, practices them with
VLM-parameterized single-axis control, and retrains the VLA on
successful segments; on a real xArm, twisting and pouring reach 92% and
96% against 32% and 16% for a zero-shot code-as-policy baseline with the
same VLM (25 trials each). Agentic Skill Discovery ([Zhao et al.,
2024](#bib.bib365)) has a language model propose the next task from its
skill library and a pool of failed tasks, and keeps a skill only after a
VLM confirms it; in simulation, RL reaches at least 90% success on 17 of
22 tabulated tasks. EmbodiedRSI ([Song et al., 2026b](#bib.bib249))
applies a related signal to an agent harness: it keeps competing code
and skill hypotheses, selects the experiments expected to distinguish
them, and learns which memories to keep according to their value for
later improvement. It is evolved entirely in simulation
(Table [11](#S3.T11 "Table 11 ‣ Physical boundary cases. ‣ 3.4 Closing the Recursive Loop ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")).

Goal exploration shows what such a signal should track.
SAGG-RIAC ([Baranes and Oudeyer, 2013](#bib.bib21)) selects regions of
the goal space where competence is changing, rather than repeatedly
sampling the goals with the lowest success. Its experiments on learning
inverse models move practice away from both mastered and unreachable
regions. Failure prediction and learning-progress estimation answer
different questions: where is the policy weak, and where is another
attempt likely to change what it can do? ALAN ([Mendonca et al.,
2023](#bib.bib194)) applies a related signal on hardware, exploring two
real-world play-kitchen setups by favoring changes it can cause to
objects and its uncertainty about predicted change. Practice Makes
Perfect ([Kumar et al., 2024](#bib.bib132)) makes the choice explicit
for parameterized skills. It estimates each skill’s competence,
extrapolates the gain from another attempt, and weighs that gain by
planned task success. Over one to three hours of reset-free practice on
a Spot arm, the fraction of evaluation tasks solved rises from 0.0 to
0.8 in one environment and from 0.53 to 0.93 in the other.

At the level of states and datasets, failure becomes useful when it can
be converted into appropriate supervision, and the clearest comparisons
fix the demonstration budget while varying where it is spent. A
criticality model trained on policy outcomes ([He et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib97)) can bias collection toward scenarios that are likely
to end in failure, such as hard initial states. The method uses
importance-sampled experience for RL and criticality-selected expert
demonstrations for imitation learning. In its two multi-round simulated
runs the predictor is retrained on the current policy’s rollouts each
round. Its evaluations span simulated locomotion and manipulation, VLA
benchmarks, and a physical banana-placement task. A high criticality
score still leaves open whether a state calls for autonomous
exploration, expert correction, or avoidance. A world model can rank the
gaps instead: RoboCoach ([Liu et al., 2026d](#bib.bib170)) imagines
where each skill expert first times out and requests demonstrations for
the highest-ranked subtask–expert pairs, and with matched demonstration
budgets success rises from 13.3% to 75.0% on a Franka and from 40.0% to
83.8% on an AgileX platform, against 30.0% and 47.5% for uniform
collection into one adapter. SAVE ([Römer et al., 2026a](#bib.bib236))
sends each expert demonstration to the task and initial state where an
ensemble’s velocity fields disagree most, reaching 47% average success
on three real Franka tasks at a fixed budget of 150 demonstrations, 8 to
25 percentage points above the baselines.

Failures can also be rebuilt or searched for in simulation. F4R ([Yu
et al., 2026b](#bib.bib341)) rebuilds each diagnosed failure as a
simulated scene for targeted practice and gains 18.75 percentage points
out of distribution on four real tasks over a budget-matched targeted
imitation baseline, and EmbodiRSI ([Lang et al., 2026](#bib.bib136))
builds task-specific simulations from deployment scenes for corrections
and demonstrations aimed at current weaknesses
(Table [11](#S3.T11 "Table 11 ‣ Physical boundary cases. ‣ 3.4 Closing the Recursive Loop ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")).
SEES ([Li et al., 2026l](#bib.bib158)) restores, in simulation, the
states before the sub-skill that most often stalls a long-horizon task
and trains that skill family with PPO against an LLM-written success
check, gaining over three rounds on RoboCasa365
(Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Reported Outcomes and Experimental Context ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")).
Q-DEG ([Zhao et al., 2026a](#bib.bib363)) searches over object
placement, camera, and lighting for diverse simulated scenes in which a
VLA sometimes fails and fine-tunes it on its own successes there,
raising average success on held-out adversarial LIBERO-Spatial scenes
from 67.2% to 80.9% for $`\pi_{0.5}`$, with a small drop on the default
scenes.

Supervision is the second decision: when experience must be acquired
physically, selection must also determine when autonomy should yield to
an expert. SAGE ([Hu et al., 2026a](#bib.bib107)) estimates
short-horizon cost and uncertainty with an ensemble of world models and
combines them into a “fear” signal, and world-model prediction error
adjusts the threshold at which an expert takes over. The resulting
interventions provide targeted data for imitation and risk-constrained
learning. Most of its evidence comes from driving simulation and replay
of Waymo driving data, while the hardware evaluation covers four
controlled indoor settings for a ground robot with twenty trials per
setting. The mechanism times expert takeover by predicted risk;
long-term, unrestricted deployment remains untested. Human-in-the-loop
deployment concentrates human attention in the same way. Sirius ([Liu
et al., 2023b](#bib.bib167)) lets people intervene during deployment and
learns from those interventions, whereas Fleet-DAgger ([Hoque et al.,
2022b](#bib.bib104)) allocates a limited number of human supervisors
across multiple robots. HIL-UMI ([Han et al., 2026](#bib.bib94)) carries
the same idea into demonstrations collected with the handheld Universal
Manipulation Interface ([Chi et al., 2024](#bib.bib53)): it queries the
current policy without executing it, collects human actions where
policy–human discrepancy indicates unfamiliar behavior, and separately
refines a progress-based advantage estimator. It takes the robot out of
demonstration collection, while human action supervision and final
hardware evaluation remain necessary. Genie Centurion ([Wang et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib287)) also updates the component that decides when to
ask. Its task sentinel flags steps not completed in time, after which
the robot rewinds for an operator’s correction, and the sentinel is
fine-tuned together with the policy each round. Across four real tasks
at matched trajectory counts, the final-round step-completion score is
0.93, against 0.53 for adversarial data collection and 0.38 for
teleoperation.

Some desired experience cannot be demonstrated at first. GLIDE ([Song
et al., 2026c](#bib.bib250)) converts anticipated and observed
teleoperation failures into executable guardrails on commands and reuses
the revised guardrails during both data collection and policy execution.
Across three physical tasks, its ten-trial collection tests rise from
zero or one successes without guardrails to seven to nine with the
selected refined guardrails. Crossed policy experiments separate the
contribution of guarded training data from that of guarded execution.
Here, selection extends to constructing the conditions under which a
demonstration can be produced at all.

Safety is the third decision. A learned runtime monitor ([Liu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib168)) can request human supervision before a predicted
failure, and safe online system identification ([Zhang et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib346)) keeps informative trajectories within certified
constraints. No single score resolves all three decisions: states with
similar failure probabilities may represent a missing skill, an
unreachable target, or an unsafe transition, so a useful rule for
physical data acquisition must combine expected learning benefit with
recoverability, the available source of supervision, and the costs of
time, resets, wear, and risk.

#### 3.2.2 Judging Outcomes

A policy that reaches new states also strains its supervision: a reward
or evaluator learned on earlier behavior may not score those states
correctly. The least invasive response is to update the judge and
rescore existing data. PEBBLE ([Lee et al., 2021](#bib.bib139)) learns a
reward model from preferences between pairs of behaviors (supplied by a
scripted teacher in its quantitative experiments) and relabels the
entire replay buffer whenever that model changes, so that off-policy
learning in its simulated locomotion and manipulation tasks always sees
one current interpretation of stored experience. RL-VLM-F ([Wang et al.,
2024c](#bib.bib293)) keeps this preference-based loop but takes the
labels from a vision-language model that compares pairs of images
against a text goal, so that its simulated tasks need no human or
scripted teacher.

FIERCE ([Tan et al., 2026b](#bib.bib263)) applies this response on
hardware: it fits and calibrates an evaluator of progress and failure on
local successes and failures. Each refinement round freezes a versioned
snapshot of the evaluator, consistently relabels the replay buffer,
updates the policy, and later refreshes the evaluator with newer
rollouts. On physical peg-in-hole and cup-stacking tasks, the reported
single-seed comparisons favor periodic refresh over a frozen task
evaluator, although total acquisition cost is not equalized. Feedback
thus stays stable during each policy update and can be revised between
updates. RLER ([Wu et al., 2026](#bib.bib301)) refits a
success-probability reward model on the policy’s own rollouts between
rounds of offline RL; on two real Franka tasks, two rounds raise success
from 64% to 84% and from 60% to 86% over the starting policy, 8 to 12
percentage points above keeping the same reward model fixed.
EvoHIL ([Zhang et al., 2026h](#bib.bib359)) retrains its reward
classifier during human-in-the-loop RL from operator-confirmed successes
and deploys each version only after a held-out accuracy gate; under a
lighting shift on six real tasks, success reaches 0.73 to 1.00 against
0.13 to 0.50 for HIL-SERL, in a comparison the authors describe as not
resource-matched. VeriFine ([Zhou et al., 2026b](#bib.bib373)) revises
the judge itself when policy gains plateau: an agent edits the judge’s
rubric and asks human experts to settle disagreements, which on
driving-reasoning data raises the judge’s correlation with human ratings
from 0.55 to 0.85 and the policy’s reasoning score from 68.05 to 83.13
under matched training budgets.

A learned world model can also act as a judge, and it inherits the blind
spots of its training data. On a physical arm, a scene-adapted
Ctrl-World model fine-tuned on successes scored 90% of held-out failing
sequences as success-like under a latent-distance diagnostic, and
fine-tuning on execution-checked counterfactual failures lowered this to
33% ([Xu et al., 2026c](#bib.bib318)). Judges that only rank a frozen
policy’s candidate actions at run time, without supervising an update,
appear with action selection in
Section [3.1.1](#S3.SS1.SSS1.Px3 "From proposals to policies. ‣ 3.1.1 Policy Updates ‣ 3.1 Improving Policies, World Models, and Knowledge ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI").

A larger change is to revise the reward specification itself. Language
models first entered this role as proxy reward functions. [Kwon et al.
(2023)](#bib.bib134) prompt a language model with a task description and
an episode outcome and use its answer as the reward in negotiation and
matrix games. Language to Rewards ([Yu et al., 2023](#bib.bib339)) has a
language model translate instructions into reward parameters that a
model-predictive controller optimizes for a simulated quadruped, a
simulated dexterous manipulator, and a real robot arm. Text2Reward ([Xie
et al., 2024](#bib.bib312)) turns a natural-language goal and an
abstract description of the environment into executable dense-reward
code; after users inspect policy rollouts, their feedback can prompt
another version of the code. Its main evaluations use simulated
manipulation and locomotion, with policies trained in simulation
demonstrated on two tasks with a Franka arm. Eureka ([Ma et al.,
2024a](#bib.bib190)) removes the human from this editing loop by
training policies under candidate rewards and returning task fitness,
together with statistics of each reward component, to the language
model. In Text2Reward and Eureka, the language model’s weights remain
fixed; improvement comes from new context and externally supplied
evaluation.

Later systems vary this loop mainly to cut its cost or to check
candidates before training. STRIDE ([Wu et al., 2025](#bib.bib303))
refines humanoid-locomotion rewards from training statistics and reports
a best success score about 2.5 times Eureka’s on random terrain in
simulation, although the two methods use different language models.
CARD ([Sun et al., 2024](#bib.bib255)) first checks whether a candidate
reward ranks recorded successes above failures and skips RL training
when it does not. It matches or exceeds expert rewards on 10 of 12
simulated tasks with about 14K tokens per task against about 663K for
Eureka. MEMENTO ([Sygkounas et al., 2026](#bib.bib260)) evolves the
evaluator before the policy, so that code-policy search in simulation
solves Tower of Hanoi in 0.97 of episodes, whereas the same search under
the unevolved evaluator solves none.

These loops also need a criterion that stays outside the quantity being
optimized. A reward program can score demonstrations sensibly yet induce
shortcut behavior during training; a quicker lift can coexist with
excessive grip force, jerky motion, or a fragile final state.
Text2Reward uses human interpretation as an anchor, while Eureka relies
on a task-fitness function specified by researchers. Without such an
independent reference, iterating on the reward can amplify a
misspecification. Revising supervision has to ask two questions: does
the new signal accelerate learning, and does the resulting behavior
still satisfy the original objective?

Training conditions can be revised as well as rewards. DrEureka ([Ma
et al., 2024b](#bib.bib191)) runs Eureka to write a reward, evaluates
the resulting policy under perturbed simulator parameters to find the
ranges in which it still performs well, and then asks a language model
to choose a domain-randomization configuration (the ranges of physical
parameters varied during simulated training) within those ranges. The
resulting policies transfer to physical quadruped and
dexterous-manipulation platforms without further real-world training.
Here the policy probes its own later training distribution, but only in
simulation; deployment experience does not feed back into that
distribution. Broadening variation can increase robustness, yet overly
wide ranges consume rollouts and can make the task unnecessarily hard to
learn.

Physical verification can instead become memory for later judgments.
REVOLVE ([Liu et al., 2026b](#bib.bib166)) stores cases in which a VLM’s
judgment of an outcome disagrees with human verification and retrieves
similar mismatches as context for future judgments. In parallel, it
updates the policy from successful rollouts and from failure–correction
data. Across four physical tasks, policy success rises over five
iterations and judgment accuracy over four memory updates, supported by
task-specific automated correction and reset routines. Because mismatch
memory, policy data, and behavior change together, the study
demonstrates a functioning dual loop without separating the contribution
of each loop.

Retrieval can alter the effective procedure even when model weights stay
fixed: ASPIRE uses earlier repairs to construct controllers, whereas
REVOLVE uses earlier judgment errors to interpret later outcomes.
FailBench ([Navasardyan et al., 2026](#bib.bib207)) measures how far
such judges can be trusted: across 2,197 real and simulated manipulation
attempts, the best of 13 VLM success detectors reaches 0.77 balanced
accuracy, and none exceeds 0.60 on contact-intensive assembly. Every
loop above that revises behavior against a learned judge is exposed to
errors of this kind, so part of the success evaluation must stay outside
the loop
(Section [4.3.2](#S4.SS3.SSS2 "4.3.2 Protecting the Judge ‣ 4.3 Keeping Improvement Safe ‣ 4 Challenges and Future Directions for Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")).

#### 3.2.3 Shaping Training Data

Once experience is collected and judged, the procedure must decide what
the next update learns from: which retained data, corrections,
demonstrations, or teacher outputs, and from which model. Several
examples below run a fixed procedure and report a later-learning
benefit; they appear here because they change where the procedure’s
training data come from. Acquired competence first changes who can
supply the next learner’s evidence. In RoboCat ([Bousmalis et al.,
2024](#bib.bib28))
(Section [3.1.1](#S3.SS1.SSS1.Px1 "From practice to training targets. ‣ 3.1.1 Policy Updates ‣ 3.1 Improving Policies, World Models, and Knowledge ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")),
an adapted specialist collects data for the next generalist; the study
demonstrates one completed cycle of this transfer. PLD ([Xiao et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib305))
(Section [3.1.1](#S3.SS1.SSS1.Px3 "From proposals to policies. ‣ 3.1.1 Policy Updates ‣ 3.1 Improving Policies, World Models, and Knowledge ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI"))
instead distills a specialist’s recoveries from the generalist’s own
deployment states back into the generalist. The useful output in both
cases is data that cover a task, a state, or a correction that the next
learner would otherwise lack.

Acquired competence can also lower the cost of later learning in roles
other than physical collection: VLAW ([Guo et al., 2026](#bib.bib90))
amplifies scarce real rollouts through a refreshed world model (below),
ASPIRE ([Lu et al., 2026a](#bib.bib180)) avoids rediscovering a working
program on a new robot API
(Section [3.1.3](#S3.SS1.SSS3.Px4 "Transferring across robots. ‣ 3.1.3 Memories, Skills, Code, and Runtimes ‣ 3.1 Improving Policies, World Models, and Knowledge ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")),
and CIDER ([Li et al., 2026d](#bib.bib148)) keeps earlier skills by
reusing the accumulated policy as a teacher
(Section [3.1.1](#S3.SS1.SSS1.Px4 "From single runs to lifelong practice. ‣ 3.1.1 Policy Updates ‣ 3.1 Improving Policies, World Models, and Knowledge ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")).
Verified solutions of coding agents can also become training data:
EmbodiedSWE ([Shen et al., 2026](#bib.bib244)) expands one simulated
solution into diverse demonstrations for a VLA, which then completes a
long-horizon task on a real robot, and HexaAnything ([Gao et al.,
2026](#bib.bib80)) trains a model on the verified execution traces of
its own agent.
Table [9](#S3.T9 "Table 9 ‣ 3.2.3 Shaping Training Data ‣ 3.2 Improving Learning Procedures ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
adds related cases from
Sections [3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Improving Policies, World Models, and Knowledge ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
and [3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Improving Learning Procedures ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
and lists, for each retained artifact, what is held fixed, the reported
comparison and effort, and the scope of the result.

Table 9: Reported later-learning comparisons, with each study’s reported
