portions of acquisition and use across studies.

A model that supplies training experience can itself be refreshed from
new physical experience. VLAW ([Guo et al., 2026](#bib.bib90)) returns
both successful and failed rollouts to world-model training, alongside
retained data from the DROID dataset ([Khazatsky et al.,
2024](#bib.bib125)), and fine-tunes a VLM-based reward model on
first-round outcomes. The updated world model then generates closed-loop
trajectories, and the VLA is trained on reward-filtered imagined
successes together with real successes. Over two rounds and five real
task categories, this full loop outperforms behavior cloning on filtered
successes (Filtered BC) and DSRL while holding the number of physical
rollouts fixed at fifty per category per round. Because model refresh,
reward calibration, and synthetic data change together, the gain belongs
to the pipeline as a whole.

Other systems refresh the practice model in the same way, and some
isolate parts of the effect. World-VLA-Loop ([Liu et al.,
2026g](#bib.bib173)) refits its video model and reward head on success
and near-success rollouts of each new policy and restarts the policy
from its fine-tuned starting point every round; on two real Franka
tasks, two rounds raise success from 13.3% to 50.0% and from 26.7% to
53.3%, the second round adding 13.3 percentage points on both.
WoVR ([Jiang et al., 2026](#bib.bib120)) refits its world model on
rollouts of the already improved policy and, at the same
2,500-trajectory budget in LIBERO, beats adding base-policy data by 5.0
percentage points; its real-robot gains were obtained without this
refresh. WorldSample ([Xue et al., 2026b](#bib.bib322)) refits a video
model on accumulating real rollouts and admits its synthetic transitions
into critic training by value balance and policy entropy, reaching 82%
average success on five real tasks against 56% for HIL-SERL with the
same demonstrations. MeRL ([Li et al., 2026h](#bib.bib152)) measures how
far its updated world model diverges from stored real continuations and
uses that error to set how much imagined data enters each update,
gaining 3.5 percentage points on LIBERO-PRO over the same simulator
updated without this trust layer. RIWANav ([Xie et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib308)), which calls itself recursive self-improvement,
lets the improved navigation policy choose which recorded action–video
pairs refit its world model, adding 7.94 percentage points of success
over a frozen world model on an offline urban-navigation benchmark.

Corrective actions can also come from outside the robot: dynamics models
learned from human video propose them at failed states, and training on
them raises success on seven real tasks across two robots from 40% to
81% ([Chen et al., 2026b](#bib.bib38)). A fixed multimodal agent can
serve as that outside teacher in a recurring loop: Local Recovery
Supervision ([Zhang et al., 2026k](#bib.bib362)) audits each round’s
policy for unresolved failures, has the agent generate recovery
demonstrations at those states, and trains the policy that drives the
next round of collection. In a preliminary simulated study on
LIBERO-Goal, recovery-augmented post-training of a $`\pi_{0}`$
checkpoint succeeds in 88 of 100 validation scenes, against 78 for
continuing on the original data with the same additional optimization
steps.

Selection also applies to experience that has already been retained, as
when Memory Anchors ([Du et al., 2026](#bib.bib65))
(Section [3.1.1](#S3.SS1.SSS1.Px4 "From single runs to lifelong practice. ‣ 3.1.1 Policy Updates ‣ 3.1 Improving Policies, World Models, and Knowledge ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI"))
enriches replay with selected old transitions. Criticality-guided
sampling
(Section [3.2.1](#S3.SS2.SSS1 "3.2.1 Choosing What to Practice ‣ 3.2 Improving Learning Procedures ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI"))
asks where new learning is most needed; Memory Anchors asks which
earlier distinctions must remain visible while that learning occurs.
Together they expose a trade-off between learning new behavior and
keeping old behavior, one that the simpler instruction to “collect hard
cases” hides.

Which gap matters also depends on the component that receives the data,
as a world-model example shows. ConfAL-WM ([Liu et al.,
2026f](#bib.bib172)) uses a confidence probe to allocate the
post-training data budget of a world model across tasks, sampling
episodes at random within each task, and gives larger training weight to
frames and image patches where the model is least reliable. Under a
fixed budget of selected data on the RoboTwin 2.0 benchmark ([Chen
et al., 2025c](#bib.bib44)), confidence-guided selection improves scene
consistency and trajectory metrics, and confidence weighting improves
reconstruction, relative to alternative acquisition scores. Whether the
same samples most improve control is a different question, since a
transition that is informative about visual prediction may differ from
one that supplies the policy with a missing action.

Rollouts can also decide which demonstrations to keep. Demo-SCORE ([Chen
et al., 2025a](#bib.bib36)) trains a success classifier on the robot’s
rollouts and removes demonstrations that resemble failures. On real
ALOHA tasks, this improves success by about 30 percentage points on
average over training on all demonstrations. CUPID ([Agia et al.,
2025](#bib.bib2)) attributes closed-loop outcomes to individual
demonstrations with influence functions and raises success on a real
Franka task from 44% to 84% with 25 curation rollouts. Both curate once
rather than as the policy changes. A model can also generate or vet its
own training data. LACY ([Hong et al., 2026b](#bib.bib102)) uses one VLM
to map language to actions, describe actions back, and judge their
agreement, and filters its own generated data with that judge.
RSI-Nav ([Li et al., 2026f](#bib.bib150)), described as data-centric
recursive self-improvement, writes instructions for unlabeled
trajectories, keeps those it can follow to the goal, and retrains before
labeling the next shard. With about 2.5M generated samples, it raises
simulated R2R-CE success from 52.9% to 68.6%. RE-0 ([Zhang et al.,
2026e](#bib.bib354)) admits a stronger teacher’s code patches into a
student’s training data only when paired rollouts from the same
simulator snapshot show a gain, which lifts robosuite restacking from
4/50 to 31/50. Its ablations credit the admitted patches rather than the
weighting of its distillation loss: on restacking, success-filtered
teacher demonstrations stay at the base level, and on a lifting task the
paired admission rule beats unfiltered and sign-only selection in every
trainer seed.

These later-learning benefits do not require the robot to learn how to
revise its learning procedure; often a fixed collection, filtering, or
distillation recipe performs the transfer.

#### 3.2.4 Constructing Updates

Once the data and supervision for an update are chosen, the update
itself is usually still computed by a fixed rule. A further step is to
change the procedure that produces the update. We use _updater_ for a
procedure that maps the learner’s current state, experience, and
objective to an operation such as a parameter step, a loss function, an
edit to a skill library, or a code patch.
Section [2.3](#S2.SS3.SSS0.Px4 "Meta-learning. ‣ 2.3 Relating RSI to Robot Learning ‣ 2 Foundations of Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
reviews precedents that learn initializations, losses, and update rules,
mostly in computation. Robot data have already trained part of an update
mechanism. [Meier et al. (2018)](#bib.bib193) learn online a memory of
learning rates that scales the gradient steps of inverse-dynamics models
on a real Kuka LWR IV arm. They reuse it as the payload changes from
none to light and heavy and reach lower prediction error early in each
task. The memory’s own learning rule stays fixed, however, and the gain
is measured in model error rather than in control. Here we follow
updaters that act on robot learners and their artifacts. AdaRSI ([Wang
et al., 2026d](#bib.bib284)), named for on-demand recursive
self-improvement, decides where an update should go. A coding agent
first refines its harness and fine-tunes the executor only on sub-steps
that stay unreliable after retries from saved states. In RoboCasa365
simulation, this raises unseen composite-task success from 4.6% to
13.8%, slightly above fine-tuning every sub-step (12.6%) at 28% of its
GPU time. Its agent also writes, from pilot tasks, an experience
document and a training budget that guide later tasks.

PRACTICE ([Bai et al., 2026](#bib.bib18)) instantiates a related idea
for an external skill library. Given trajectories and the current
library, its learned editor can add, revise, merge, or remove skill
entries, while a frozen executor uses the resulting library. The
editor’s training progresses from successful oracle trajectories,
through paired success and failure examples, to on-policy distillation
from a stronger frozen teacher on the student’s own editing contexts. On
the simulated EB-ALFRED household tasks from EmbodiedBench ([Yang
et al., 2025](#bib.bib329)), the failure-aware stage reaches 45.3%
average success, compared with 42.7% for a control trained only on
successes, supporting the value of failures for training the editor. The
broader gains across stages are harder to attribute, because the editor,
its training data, and the accumulated library change together. What has
improved is the editor; the executor, the external teacher, and the
staged procedure that trains the editor all remain fixed.

When the value of a proposed change can only be established through
robot interaction, constructing updates becomes inseparable from safe
execution, resets, measurement, and recovery.

#### 3.2.5 Automating Experiments

[TABLE]

Table 10: Changes to collection, supervision, update, and experimental
procedures.

An updater can propose a new policy, loss, or training routine, but a
physical system can judge that proposal only by running another
experiment. Each candidate must begin from a known state, remain within
safety limits, be deployed under recorded conditions, and receive an
outcome that is sufficiently independent of the code being tested.
Resets make successive trials comparable; verification supplies the
selection signal; and logging connects a measured change to the
hypothesis that produced it. These services belong to the learning loop
itself.

ENPIRE ([Xiao et al., 2026b](#bib.bib306)) instantiates this loop for
research on robot policies. In a human-guided construction stage, coding
agents build task-specific services for safety, resets, and
verification. The finalized services are then exposed as interfaces that
cannot be modified, while coding agents revise the permitted training
infrastructure or policy code, launch robot rollouts, inspect
trajectories and videos, and retain or abandon hypotheses based on the
resulting measurements. This covers more of the research process than
executing a fixed fine-tuning script, while keeping the main outcome
check outside the policy code that can be changed. Its autonomy still
depends on the supplied task objective, demonstrations, hardware, and
interface boundaries, and a misspecified verifier could consistently
select the wrong revision.

ENPIRE studies two ways to extend a single experimental loop. Running
more agent–robot pairs in parallel buys throughput at a resource cost;
whether it also improves the updater is a separate question. In a
separate transfer, agents distill their search on a pin-insertion task
into a written summary and append it to the instructions for a
GPU-insertion task, while removing prior trajectories, logs, and
checkpoints. The result shows that procedural knowledge can be carried
between related experiments; measuring how much that knowledge improves
the later search would need a matched run without the summary.

Agents increasingly run the training pipeline itself. In simulation, a
coding agent ran more than 70 quadruped-locomotion experiments in
fourteen waves under human high-level direction ([Khandelwal and Gupta,
2026](#bib.bib124)). HARBOR ([Li et al., 2026i](#bib.bib155)) stages
simulator setup, reward design, and tuning through gated sub-agents and
appends distilled lessons to an experience memory, reaching 0.885
success on three-cube stacking in IsaacLab where Eureka and REvolve
reach 0.0 under the same model and wall-clock budget. AURA ([Zhu et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib376)) has language-model agents write staged curricula
that specify rewards, domain randomization, and PPO settings, trains
each stage in MJX simulation, and refines the next stage from its
analysis, retrieving earlier curricula and feedback from a database; its
hardware deployment on a custom humanoid is reported qualitatively.
RoboClaw ([Li et al., 2026e](#bib.bib149)) pairs each forward
manipulation with an inverse recovery behavior so that a dual-arm mobile
manipulator can reset itself and keep collecting data, while one VLM
agent coordinates collection, policy learning, and execution. It reports
about 25% higher long-horizon success than its baselines, without
stating whether the gain is absolute. It also reports that a manual
baseline needs about 2.16 times its human time for the same amount of
data. The RoboCoach system ([Lei et al., 2026](#bib.bib143)), unrelated
to the world-model coach of
Section [3.2.1](#S3.SS2.SSS1 "3.2.1 Choosing What to Practice ‣ 3.2 Improving Learning Procedures ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI"),
pairs a coding agent with a video-reading feedback agent: on
RoboCoach-Bench, a set of 32 simulated tasks, the seven-model mean
success reaches 0.730 against 0.602 for expert codebases, and on four
real tasks in two laboratories the resulting policies reach 0.68 against
0.51 for matched human configurations.

Two studies measure what such loops still need. An agentic loop with
evidence-gated promotion ([Yu, 2026](#bib.bib336)) cuts false promotions
in LIBERO-10 simulation to 0.001 per run. Yet on its one measured
lineage, its selections trail simply taking the final checkpoint (about
50–54% against 60% held-out success). Coding agents in RLE-Bench ([Ma
et al., 2026](#bib.bib186)) likewise gain on the development evaluations
they can query but lose verifier score on hidden robustness
perturbations in simulation.

EndoRSI ([Ng et al., 2026](#bib.bib208)) brings a human-governed coding
agent to an endoscopic robot: benchtop phantom trials rejected an
insertion strategy that offline data had supported, and benchtop
insertion success rose from 2/21 to 17/21 over four generations of
revised policies.

Neighboring fields have automated other parts of the experimental loop.
The AI Scientist ([Lu et al., 2024](#bib.bib178)) automates proposal,
execution, analysis, and reporting in digital experiments. Robotic
chemistry closes a physical loop within more structured apparatus: a
mobile robotic chemist ([Burger et al., 2020](#bib.bib33)) and the
A-Lab ([Szymanski et al., 2023](#bib.bib261)) select experiments,
manipulate materials, and incorporate measured synthesis or
characterization outcomes, while Coscientist ([Boiko et al.,
2023](#bib.bib26)) adds planning and tool use by a language model.
Across these settings, a reusable finding requires the candidate
version, initial conditions, operating configuration, measurements, and
failed trials to remain attributable.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### 3.3 Improving the Improver

This section discusses mechanisms through which an improver could
improve and the evidence offered for them. An improver’s knowledge may
reside in weights, retrieved memory, code, or prompts
(Section [2.2](#S2.SS2 "2.2 Defining Recursive Self-Improvement ‣ 2 Foundations of Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")).
After stating what would count as improvement, we group mechanisms by
where that knowledge lives.

##### What would count as a better improver.

As
Section [2.2](#S2.SS2 "2.2 Defining Recursive Self-Improvement ‣ 2 Foundations of Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
notes, successively better procedures can come from a fixed outer
searcher. One example is a loop that its authors call policy-level
recursive self-improvement: a criticality model updated from each
round’s outcomes guides the next collection, but the update rule stays
fixed ([He et al., 2026a](#bib.bib97)). An improver can also revise its
own selection rules, such as how strict its admission gate is or which
failures it debugs next; such a change alters the procedure that
improves the system, yet it counts toward recursion only if the revised
rules produce better later revisions than the earlier ones.

The missed grasp illustrates the difference between procedure
improvement and recursion. Suppose a rollout reveals a visual signature
of slip in an attempt that the reward program scored as a success. Using
that signature to correct the reward and training a better policy under
it would demonstrate procedure improvement. Here the reward program
belongs to the learning procedure, the editor that writes it is the
improver, and the records it keeps from such edits are its repair
knowledge. The recursive route must also retain which failure
distinction motivated the edit, under what conditions the edit was
valid, and whether the downstream learner benefited. Those records could
revise the reward editor’s parameters, retrieval memory, or
rule-selection policy. The first link is present if the revised editor’s
rewards for new failures teach matched learners better than the earlier
editor’s rewards do. The second link is present if, given the same new
repair histories, a revision of the editor proposed with what it has
learned outperforms both the unrevised editor and a revision of the same
editor proposed with that knowledge frozen.

The test leaves room for people and fixed machinery: human-specified
goals, a fixed experiment runner, and an independently controlled safety
boundary may remain in place. What must be traced is the source of the
useful revision. If the gains came only from more trials, compute, or
human assistance, a frozen-knowledge control given the same resources
would match the updated version.

Against this standard, the physical systems covered by this review offer
mechanisms and uncontrolled results for R1. We have not found sufficient
evidence that freezes the acquired revision knowledge, matches the
conditions of later learning, and isolates an R1 gain on new failures
(Sections [4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Measuring Improvement ‣ 4 Challenges and Future Directions for Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
and [4.4](#S4.SS4.SSS0.Px6 "How to test recursion. ‣ 4.4 Making Improvement Recursive ‣ 4 Challenges and Future Directions for Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI"));
the closest results, described next, come from simulation and do not yet
meet all three conditions.

##### Learning from repair histories.

Several systems already keep records of earlier revisions and consult
them when revising again, which places knowledge in the improver’s
memory. AdaRSI’s ([Wang et al., 2026d](#bib.bib284)) coding agent
writes, after pilot tasks, an experience document recording which
sub-steps benefited from training and how much data sufficed, together
with a training budget, and both guide later tasks
(Section [3.2.4](#S3.SS2.SSS4 "3.2.4 Constructing Updates ‣ 3.2 Improving Learning Procedures ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")).
HARBOR ([Li et al., 2026i](#bib.bib155)) distills recurring patterns
from tuning rounds into an experience memory that later reward design
and tuning retrieve
(Section [3.2.5](#S3.SS2.SSS5 "3.2.5 Automating Experiments ‣ 3.2 Improving Learning Procedures ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")).
Drawing on its accumulated experience in a separate run, it redesigns
the reward for simulated three-cube stacking in 30 minutes rather than 4
hours, but on the same task and without a frozen-memory control; its
ablation without experience removes templates, references, and
heuristics, so the contribution of the lessons it accumulates on its own
is not separated. AURA ([Zhu et al., 2025a](#bib.bib376)) stores earlier
curricula, metrics, and human feedback in a database that conditions
later curriculum, reward, and training-configuration generation
(Section [3.2.5](#S3.SS2.SSS5 "3.2.5 Automating Experiments ‣ 3.2 Improving Learning Procedures ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI"));
without the database, the share of its generated curricula that launch
training in simulation falls from 99% to 38% with GPT-4.1, but what AURA
acquired itself is not separated from the human feedback.
EmbodiedRSI ([Song et al., 2026b](#bib.bib249)) learns which memories to
keep according to their value for later improvement
(Section [3.2.1](#S3.SS2.SSS1 "3.2.1 Choosing What to Practice ‣ 3.2 Improving Learning Procedures ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI"));
on unseen RoboCasa365 composite tasks in simulation, this learned rule
reaches 71.3% success against 61.7% for retrieval-based selection, a
comparison of memory rules rather than of acquired knowledge.
ENPIRE ([Xiao et al., 2026b](#bib.bib306)) carries a written summary of
one search into the instructions for a related task
(Section [3.2.5](#S3.SS2.SSS5 "3.2.5 Automating Experiments ‣ 3.2 Improving Learning Procedures ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")).
In each case the improver’s knowledge changes; what remains to be shown
is that this change, rather than added trials, compute, or human input,
makes the next procedure better.

Two kinds of reuse sit close to R1 without reaching it. ASPIRE ([Lu
et al., 2026a](#bib.bib180)) retrieves guidance from earlier program
repairs, and the code-transfer study ([Kuroki and Tang,
2026](#bib.bib133)) supplies optimized programs as references; both
improve how a fixed coding model constructs later task controllers
(Section [3.1.3](#S3.SS1.SSS3.Px2 "Reusing skills and code. ‣ 3.1.3 Memories, Skills, Code, and Runtimes ‣ 3.1 Improving Policies, World Models, and Knowledge ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")),
which is evidence about constructing behavior rather than about revising
collection, supervision, or updates. LMPC ([Liang et al.,
2024](#bib.bib160)) trains the model that writes reward code for a
model-predictive controller on past teaching sessions, so that teaching
needs fewer turns. In simulation, a successful session on unseen tasks
takes 1.9 rather than 2.4 chat turns
(Section [2.3](#S2.SS3.SSS0.Px4 "Meta-learning. ‣ 2.3 Relating RSI to Robot Learning ‣ 2 Foundations of Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")).
That reward code drives real-time control rather than an RL training
run, and the recipe that trains the model stays fixed.
HarnessPAI’s ([Wang et al., 2026g](#bib.bib289)) growing library of
failure-to-repair notes plays the role of ASPIRE’s guidance for its
program writer: in simulation, three LIBERO-Object tasks reach full
success within two rounds with the library rather than several without
it, but no frozen-library comparison on new failures separates what the
writer has gained
(Section [3.1.3](#S3.SS1.SSS3.Px3 "Revising the runtime. ‣ 3.1.3 Memories, Skills, Code, and Runtimes ‣ 3.1 Improving Policies, World Models, and Knowledge ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")).

##### Revising the tools that revise.

PhysEvo ([Tian et al., 2026](#bib.bib270)), which its authors describe
as physical recursive self-improvement, keeps a single frozen model but
lets a meta-agent revise the task agent’s tools and skills and also its
own diagnostic tools. In simulation it reaches 62.0% on held-out
RoboDojo layouts, an equal-weight average over five capability
dimensions, against 47.2% computed from public evaluation records for
the strongest published comparison; on a real arm it succeeds in 84% of
25 trials while skill revision continues. It is the clearest physical
case of an improver that edits its own instruments; the comparison that
would attribute part of the gain to those edits, the same meta-agent
with its diagnostic tools frozen, remains to be run.

Admission rules are another instrument an improver uses. When an
optimizer agent revises a robot agent’s harness in simulated LIBERO
tasks, a champion–challenger rule avoids the degradation that accepting
every revision causes ([Wei et al., 2026b](#bib.bib298)).
RegenHarness ([Wang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib281)) forbids its updater to
weaken its own acceptance rule. In both cases the designers set the
admission rule, so these results show which instrument an improver
should use rather than an improver that improves it. MEMENTO ([Sygkounas
et al., 2026](#bib.bib260)) evolves its rollout evaluator once before
policy search, and VeriFine ([Zhou et al., 2026b](#bib.bib373)) revises
its judge’s rubric with human calibration
(Section [3.2.2](#S3.SS2.SSS2 "3.2.2 Judging Outcomes ‣ 3.2 Improving Learning Procedures ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI"));
both change an instrument through a fixed process, which places them at
procedure improvement unless the process that revises the instrument
itself improves. STOP ([Zelikman et al., 2024](#bib.bib344)) is the
digital reference point for such self-application. It applies a
language-model-driven improver program to itself; with GPT-4, the
self-improved improver raises held-out performance over a few rounds and
transfers to new tasks without further optimization, whereas weaker
models degrade, and the authors note that the unchanged language model
makes this less than full recursive self-improvement. SICA ([Robeyns
et al., 2025](#bib.bib234)) removes the split between meta-agent and
target agent: the best agent so far edits its own codebase, and in one
fifteen-iteration run with Claude 3.5 Sonnet, peak accuracy on a fixed
50-question SWE-bench Verified subset rose from 17% to 53%, with the
same benchmarks used for selection and for reporting. A fixed base agent
that makes every edit is the control that would separate better task
tools from a better editor. VERSE ([Wang et al., 2026k](#bib.bib295))
lets a harness optimizer revise its own prompts, skills, tools, and
notes as well as the executor’s harness, with model weights fixed. In
its controlled study on held-out SWE-rebench tasks (one run per
condition), self-revision without execution-based checks produced no
harness that beat the initial one on validation, whereas with such
checks it reached 41.05% against 39.20% for a fixed optimizer and 39.81%
for checks alone; revising the reviser helped only when its edits could
be tested. Predict Before You Modify ([Xie et al., 2026d](#bib.bib313))
adds to a self-modifying agent an editable model that predicts the
outcome of each proposed modification and is revised from earlier
modifications and their observed results; its robotics domain is
quadruped reward design in the Genesis simulator, and its control with
the predictor frozen, run on coding tasks, has bootstrap intervals that
include zero.

##### Carrying repair knowledge across tasks and robots.

R1 needs repair knowledge that transfers beyond the failures that
produced it
(Section [4.4](#S4.SS4.SSS0.Px3 "Transferring repair knowledge. ‣ 4.4 Making Improvement Recursive ‣ 4 Challenges and Future Directions for Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")),
and the evidence so far concerns mostly task-level artifacts. ASPIRE
carries guidance from simulated Franka repairs to a bimanual robot with
a different API
(Section [3.1.3](#S3.SS1.SSS3.Px4 "Transferring across robots. ‣ 3.1.3 Memories, Skills, Code, and Runtimes ‣ 3.1 Improving Policies, World Models, and Knowledge ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")),
and ENPIRE’s written summary moves from pin insertion to GPU insertion
on real robots without a matched control. A simulated study of 123
rounds of agentic skill discovery ([Wang, 2026](#bib.bib279)) shows how
accumulated revisions can stall: deployed changes kept passing their
tests while the target task never succeeded. MC-EvoBench ([Song et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib248)) sets out the controls a transfer claim needs: the
target world and inventory are reset, only a declared artifact carries
over, and related experience is compared with no-prior, unrelated, and
shuffled sources at matched environment steps. In Minecraft, over five
seeds, a memory-based agent showed no stable transfer, and related
experience lowered stone-tool stage success from 0.150 to 0.050.
Applying the frozen-knowledge comparison of
Section [4.4](#S4.SS4.SSS0.Px6 "How to test recursion. ‣ 4.4 Making Improvement Recursive ‣ 4 Challenges and Future Directions for Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
across failure families or robots remains to be run.

### 3.4 Closing the Recursive Loop

R2 asks for the last step: the improver, once improved and using what it
has acquired, must help produce a next version that is better than
itself
(Section [2.2](#S2.SS2 "2.2 Defining Recursive Self-Improvement ‣ 2 Foundations of Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")).
Digital systems supply the closest precedents, because executable tests
make each candidate cheap to judge, while physical systems supply
boundary cases; the gap between the two points to the paths ahead. In
the physical systems covered by this review, we have not found a
controlled comparison that isolates an R2 contribution; the closest
controlled evidence comes from a simulated reward-design task in a
digital system, discussed below.

##### Digital precedents.

Digital systems also separate applying a fixed update recipe from making
the updater itself an object of search. Expert Iteration ([Anthony
et al., 2017](#bib.bib12)) alternates tree search with training a
network to imitate the search, then uses that network to guide the next
search; STaR ([Zelikman et al., 2022](#bib.bib343)) repeatedly generates
rationales, keeps those that lead to correct answers, and fine-tunes on
them. Both repeat a fixed loop. Promptbreeder ([Fernando et al.,
2024](#bib.bib78)) evolves both task prompts and the mutation prompts
that change them. ADAS ([Hu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib110)) searches over
agent designs written as code, and ALMA ([Xiong et al.,
2026](#bib.bib315)) searches over memory designs written as code and
finds designs that outperform human-crafted ones in four sequential
decision-making domains. AlphaEvolve ([Novikov et al.,
2025](#bib.bib210)) couples code proposals from language models to
executable evaluators.

The Darwin Gödel Machine (DGM) ([Zhang et al., 2026c](#bib.bib350)),
which comes closest to the second link, modifies its own agent code and
keeps an archive of variants. In an ablation in which a fixed base agent
performs every modification, gains taper off quickly, whereas letting
improved agents modify themselves sustains improvement on its coding
benchmarks. That ablation is the closest analogue of the second link
that we found. It differs from the physical case in three ways: the
improver and the task solver are the same agent; the benchmark that
selects each modification also measures it, although the discovered
improvements also transfer to a held-out benchmark and to other
foundation models; and executable tests reject candidates cheaply.

Other digital systems extend the pattern. Gödel Agent ([Yin et al.,
2025](#bib.bib335)) lets an agent rewrite the code that performs its own
improvement
(Section [2.3](#S2.SS3.SSS0.Px6 "Where recursion adds a requirement. ‣ 2.3 Relating RSI to Robot Learning ‣ 2 Foundations of Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")).
SelfSearch ([Yang et al., 2026c](#bib.bib328)) has agents modify
themselves using records of earlier self-modification episodes, without
downstream reward during the search, and improves population-mean
success over the initial agent in all six model–benchmark settings it
reports. HyperAgents ([Zhang et al., 2026d](#bib.bib351)) make the meta
agent itself editable and run the fixed-improver control. With the
initial meta agent held fixed for the same number of iterations, the
median test score in simulated quadruped reward design reaches 0.213
against 0.372 when the meta agent improves itself (five runs each).
Hyperagents transferred to Olympiad-level math grading and run with
their meta agent fixed yield an improvement of 0.630 where the initial
agent yields none. In AIDE² ([Srikanth et al., 2026](#bib.bib252)), a
fixed outer-loop agent rewrites a research agent’s code, and the seven
accepted improvements transfer to four held-out benchmarks. When the
evolved agent instead drives the outer loop, its final grade is close to
that of the human-designed driver (0.780 against 0.782 over three
seeds), a result its authors call inconclusive.

Other routes make the improver a learned component. Randomly initialized
learned optimizers can train one another and, once better, speed up
their own training ([Metz et al., 2021](#bib.bib198)), and a
self-referential weight matrix modifies its own weights, including the
transformations that generate later modifications, although its authors
leave a dedicated measurement of self-improvement to future work ([Irie
et al., 2022](#bib.bib115)). MASS ([Lee et al., 2026a](#bib.bib138))
fine-tunes one model that proposes, executes, and judges multi-agent
workflows on its own traces; when workflows from two generations are run
by the same base executor, those of the newer generation win 64% of
comparisons, although discovery still used each generation’s own
executor and judge, and its robotics tasks are simulated. SpecRSI ([Xu
et al., 2026d](#bib.bib319)) trains its improver on completed searches
with the outer update rule fixed and runs the original and the updated
improver on the same released artifact, where the updated improver
yields a gain of 6.9 against 5.7 percentage points; some of its
joint-update conditions have unequal training cost.

Two recent systems sharpen what an R2 test must measure. The
Huxley-Gödel Machine ([Wang et al., 2026f](#bib.bib288)) reports that an
agent’s own benchmark score only weakly predicts how good its
self-modified descendants will be (weighted correlations of 0.27 to
0.44), whereas a score pooled over its descendants predicts it better
(0.63 to 0.78). Selecting by that pooled score, with the starting agent
and an 800-evaluation budget held fixed, its best agent reaches 56.7% on
a 60-task SWE-bench Verified subset against 53.3% for DGM and 50.0% for
SICA in single runs, and improves from 34.8% to 40.1% on 207 held-out
SWE-bench Lite tasks. The Red Queen Gödel Machine ([Iacob et al.,
2026](#bib.bib113)) lets learned evaluators evolve alongside the agents
they score and promotes an evaluator only when it beats the incumbent on
a fixed ground-truth anchor. Against frozen evaluators, in one run per
arm, its coder passes 82.1% against 75.0% of 28 held-out tasks (a winner
found with more search tokens); in a simulated Unitree Go2 reward-design
task, its mean held-out jump height is 0.365 against 0.306 m over five
runs per arm. Its comparison isolates evaluator co-evolution while the
meta-agent is editable in both arms, so, unlike DGM and HyperAgents,
neither the Huxley-Gödel Machine nor the Red Queen Gödel Machine
compares improved agents modifying themselves with a fixed base agent
making every modification at a matched budget.

##### Physical boundary cases.

Several robot systems, some evaluated only in simulation, are described
by their authors as recursive self-improvement or recursive improvement:
the criticality model’s policy-level RSI, EndoRSI, EmbodiRSI, Local
Recovery Supervision, MobiAgent, RegenHarness, Embodied Turing Machines,
RE-0, AdaRSI, PhysEvo, D-World, RIWANav, and RSI-Nav; EmbodiedRSI and
RoboRSI use the term in their names.
Table [11](#S3.T11 "Table 11 ‣ Physical boundary cases. ‣ 3.4 Closing the Recursive Loop ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
lists what each changes, where it was tested, and where this review
discusses it. Judged by the claims of
Section [2.2](#S2.SS2 "2.2 Defining Recursive Self-Improvement ‣ 2 Foundations of Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI"),
they revise policies, models, skills, data, or procedures, and several
also accumulate knowledge that guides their next revision
(Section [3.3](#S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2 "Learning from repair histories. ‣ 3.3 Improving the Improver ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")).
PhysEvo, whose meta-agent edits its own diagnostic tools, comes closest
in mechanism
(Section [3.3](#S3.SS3.SSS0.Px3 "Revising the tools that revise. ‣ 3.3 Improving the Improver ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")).
Turning any of them into evidence for R2 would require the R2 comparison
of
Section [2.2](#S2.SS2 "2.2 Defining Recursive Self-Improvement ‣ 2 Foundations of Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI"),
run on held-out failures with matched learners.

##### Paths toward physical RSI.

Four design requirements follow from the physical constraints discussed
above. First, a protected success evaluation, with an outcome check that
stays outside what the improver can change
(Section [4.3.2](#S4.SS3.SSS2 "4.3.2 Protecting the Judge ‣ 4.3 Keeping Improvement Safe ‣ 4 Challenges and Future Directions for Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")).
Second, staged evaluation: candidate revisions are screened in
simulation or on stored traces, and hardware trials go to matched
learners for the few that survive
(Section [4.4](#S4.SS4.SSS0.Px7 "What the test must control. ‣ 4.4 Making Improvement Recursive ‣ 4 Challenges and Future Directions for Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")).
Third, repair records that carry their conditions of applicability, so
that the improver can tell when an earlier lesson no longer holds
(Section [4.4](#S4.SS4.SSS0.Px3 "Transferring repair knowledge. ‣ 4.4 Making Improvement Recursive ‣ 4 Challenges and Future Directions for Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")).
Fourth, a budget that counts trials, resets, wear, and supervision,
because revision histories accumulate slowly when each entry costs
physical rounds
(Section [2.4](#S2.SS4 "2.4 Facing Physical Limits ‣ 2 Foundations of Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")).
A roadmap of autonomy levels ([Duan et al., 2026](#bib.bib69)) separates
structural recursion, in which a revised improver, verifier, or
successor generator is merely inherited, from effective recursion, in
which it produces better later improvements. In its own scheme of
levels, the roadmap places embodied intelligence at the frontier of
choosing improvement strategies and acquiring experience, with
deployment adaptation shown mainly in simulation. Reaching the top level
of the concurrent scheme in
Section [2.2](#S2.SS2 "2.2 Defining Recursive Self-Improvement ‣ 2 Foundations of Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI") ([Zhou
et al., 2026a](#bib.bib371)) would require comparisons such as those
designed in
Section [4.4](#S4.SS4.SSS0.Px4 "Testing recursive improvement. ‣ 4.4 Making Improvement Recursive ‣ 4 Challenges and Future Directions for Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI").

## 4 Challenges and Future Directions for Physical RSI

This section turns to what stands in the way of physical RSI.
Section [4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Measuring Improvement ‣ 4 Challenges and Future Directions for Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
asks what current evaluation cannot yet measure and how judges can stay
aligned as behavior improves;
Section [4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Accumulating Improvement ‣ 4 Challenges and Future Directions for Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
explains why observed gains saturate, regress, or fail to carry forward,
and how retained improvements can survive system change and finite
resources; and
Section [4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Keeping Improvement Safe ‣ 4 Challenges and Future Directions for Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
asks how practice can stay safe across rounds.
Section [4.4](#S4.SS4 "4.4 Making Improvement Recursive ‣ 4 Challenges and Future Directions for Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
sets out what stands between current results and verified recursion,
from locating the bottleneck and choosing a usable experiment to
learning a transferable repair principle and testing whether it makes
improvement recursive.
Table [12](#S4.T12 "Table 12 ‣ 4 Challenges and Future Directions for Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
lists, for each open problem, the conditions it serves, its central
question, and a starting benchmark.

Table 12: The open problems of this section at a glance, in the order of
the subsections that discuss them.
![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
marks the main focus of each direction among the four conditions:
informative feedback (IF), usability (U), robustness to distribution
shift (DS), and continued practice (CP). Starting benchmarks are
proposals from the corresponding discussions.

### 4.1 Measuring Improvement

Section [2.5](#S2.SS5 "2.5 Benchmarking Self-Improvement ‣ 2 Foundations of Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
described the benchmarks and metrics in use; this subsection asks what
they miss. Benchmarks test a system at one point in time, whereas
self-improvement unfolds over rounds, so the test tasks must stay
outside what the revising system can tune against. HarnessPAI reports
96.5% on LIBERO-PRO evaluation seeds that include its development seeds,
and RoboRSI improves online on its evaluation tasks while its baselines
do not. In RLE-Bench ([Ma et al., 2026](#bib.bib186)), coding agents
improve on the development evaluations they can query but lose 19 to 41
points of verifier score, out of 100, on hidden robustness perturbations
in simulation. Held-out seeds, tasks, and perturbations that the
revising system never queries are part of a protected success
evaluation. A held-out set also loses its validity when its results are
reused repeatedly to select candidates, because the selection can
overfit the held-out set itself ([Dwork et al., 2015](#bib.bib70)).

Comparisons across rounds are rarer than single-round gains. Behavioral
improvement is widely established
(Tables [6](#S3.T6 "Table 6 ‣ From proposals to policies. ‣ 3.1.1 Policy Updates ‣ 3.1 Improving Policies, World Models, and Knowledge ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")–[8](#S3.T8 "Table 8 ‣ Reusing skills and code. ‣ 3.1.3 Memories, Skills, Code, and Runtimes ‣ 3.1 Improving Policies, World Models, and Knowledge ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")),
but later-learning and procedure claims need matched learners
(Section [2.2](#S2.SS2 "2.2 Defining Recursive Self-Improvement ‣ 2 Foundations of Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")).
Few studies supply them. PLD does so for the training value of collected
data on hardware, and FIERCE, RLER, WoVR, SAVE, and the
demonstration-requesting RoboCoach do so for single procedure
components. Integrated pipelines such as VLAW and the RoboCoach
system ([Lei et al., 2026](#bib.bib143)), whose coding agent changes
architecture, data augmentation, optimization, and validation code
together, improve as a whole, and most results cover only the few rounds
reported. For recursion, three judgments must be kept apart: a component
of the procedure changes; the improver’s knowledge or tools change, as
in AdaRSI, HARBOR, AURA, or PhysEvo; and a recursive gain is isolated by
a frozen-knowledge or fixed-improver control with matched learners and
budgets. The physical systems reviewed here reach the second judgment at
most, while digital systems such as the Darwin Gödel Machine and
HyperAgents run fixed-improver controls with executable tests or in
simulation rather than through physical trials.
Table [13](#S4.T13 "Table 13 ‣ 4.1 Measuring Improvement ‣ 4 Challenges and Future Directions for Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
summarizes where the reviewed studies stand on each claim.

Table 13: Where the reviewed studies stand on each claim of
Section [2.2](#S2.SS2 "2.2 Defining Recursive Self-Improvement ‣ 2 Foundations of Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI").
Systems are representative and follow the assessments in the sections
that discuss them; those without an icon are digital.

When retained knowledge enters a decision rather than weights, the
corresponding measure is a component test that holds the decision-maker
fixed and varies only the retained resource. ASPIRE ([Lu et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib180)) compares debugging a real robot’s controller with
and without transferred repair guidance, although whether starting
programs and debugging budgets were matched is not stated;
REVOLVE’s ([Liu et al., 2026b](#bib.bib166)) memory instead enters
outcome judgments, so its test would compare judgments of the same
observations under old and updated memory, a pathway that its reported
judgment–policy trajectories do not isolate.

Even a well-designed comparison establishes improvement only relative to
the success judgments made by a person, sensor, or model. Hardware
studies differ in whether that channel is independent of the signal used
for learning. RoboCat ([Bousmalis et al., 2024](#bib.bib28)) uses
learned reward models for autonomous success detection and relabeling,
but counts final evaluation outcomes manually. In SILVR’s real-robot
experiments ([Luo et al., 2026a](#bib.bib182)), human judgments supply
both the filtering signal and the evaluation outcome.
Q-Planning ([Giridhar et al., 2026](#bib.bib86)) goes further: a
human-provided label supplies the terminal reward on the real robot, and
its per-iteration success rates are computed from the same collection
episodes. Each protocol supports a different claim. A shared judge can
measure improvement against its own criterion but cannot reveal a
systematic error in that criterion; an independent outcome audit tests
that additional link. The same caution applies to an agent’s own report
of completion: in the GPT-6-Astra evaluation ([Cai et al.,
2026](#bib.bib34)), self-reported progress diverged from the actual
completion conditions on simulated tasks, and its proposed benchmark
keeps judging the trajectory after the agent declares that it is done.

Tables [6](#S3.T6 "Table 6 ‣ From proposals to policies. ‣ 3.1.1 Policy Updates ‣ 3.1 Improving Policies, World Models, and Knowledge ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")–[10](#S3.T10 "Table 10 ‣ 3.2.5 Automating Experiments ‣ 3.2 Improving Learning Procedures ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
separate execution from outcome judgment for this reason. Final scorers,
or their separation from training, remain unclear for SOAR, SI-EFM,
RAPolicy, SARM2, VERITAS’s hardware tests, CIDER, RISE, PlayWorld,
HIL-SERL, PLD’s hardware tests, and VLAW. SI-EFM’s collection labels and
VLAW’s human filter audit do not establish independent final checks.
DexTouch-WM specifies five human raters for its model-evaluation
comparison; their role in the later mixed-data policy test is not
separately stated.

Success-evaluation details are also unresolved for Robo-Cortex, Zeva,
ReSYNC, ASPIRE, Uni-Skill, Criticality model, and GLIDE. REVOLVE
provides human-referenced judgment accuracy without specifying the final
policy judge. FIERCE reports independent terminal checks but
insufficient detail to assess separation. These are reporting gaps, not
evidence of incorrect judgments.

A success rate should be read with the number of trials and independent
training runs behind it. A few trials leave a wide interval even at
perfect success, and trials that share scenes, resets, checkpoints, or
training runs are less independent than a binomial calculation assumes.
Reports should therefore state trial and run counts, how tasks, initial
states, and checkpoints were selected, and whether judges agreed or were
blinded ([Kress-Gazit et al., 2024](#bib.bib130)). Differences between
methods should carry their own uncertainty. Sequential designs lower the
cost: AnyRank ([Badithela et al., 2026](#bib.bib17)) assigns more trials
to policies that are hard to separate and needs up to 50% fewer hardware
evaluations than earlier rigorous rankings. RoboArena ([Atreya et al.,
2025](#bib.bib15)) instead ranks policies from double-blind pairwise
comparisons crowd-sourced across seven institutions on the DROID
platform, and AutoEval ([Zhou et al., 2025d](#bib.bib375)) supplies
automatic success detection and scene resets so that real-world
evaluation runs with little human involvement.

A cost comparison is meaningful only once the outcome and its
uncertainty are specified. Cost accounting should separate setup and
signal construction, acquisition of the revision, downstream training
and evaluation, deployment, and later maintenance. ASPIRE reports model
tokens to the first working program or to budget exhaustion, a measure
that excludes robot time and total system cost. VLAW matches 50 physical
rollouts per task category per round against its downstream baselines,
while also fitting models and generating synthetic data. FIERCE reports
300 refinement rollouts per condition on each real task and explicitly
excludes initialization, evaluator adaptation, calibration, evaluation,
resets, and interventions from that count. These scopes answer useful
but different questions, and ranking costs across studies would mix
them.
Table [9](#S3.T9 "Table 9 ‣ 3.2.3 Shaping Training Data ‣ 3.2 Improving Learning Procedures ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
preserves the reported scope; a complete comparison of the cost to reach
a target would additionally count robot episodes and hours, resets and
human time, compute or tokens, failed runs, and revalidation after later
updates. Elapsed time belongs in this count too, because simulated
benchmarks can pause while a model deliberates: in the GPT-6-Astra
evaluation ([Cai et al., 2026](#bib.bib34)), the standard RoboDojo
budgets correspond to 8–76 s of commanded motion against an average of
55 minutes of computation, so a larger step budget raises simulated
success at no cost in elapsed time. On a real Unitree G1 humanoid, about
90% of each run went to deliberation and one manipulation trial took
over an hour, and protective stops and actuator overheating ended trials
on other robots. Its proposed benchmark therefore charges deliberation
on a world clock that keeps running.

##### Keeping judges aligned.

Measurement inside the learning loop raises a related problem: an
experiment becomes misleading if the supervision used to judge it no
longer resolves the failures produced by the improved policy. The
measurement of the task may then need to evolve without silently
changing the task itself. An early grasping policy may mostly miss the
object, so a coarse lift detector is informative. A stronger policy may
lift the object faster while squeezing hard enough to damage it. Adding
force-sensitive evidence can refine the measurement of the original
intent (a secure lift without damage), whereas redefining success to
favor speed despite damage changes the intended outcome. An evaluator
update should state which task requirements remain unchanged and which
previously missed failure modes it now detects.

Because behavior shifts toward subtler failures, an evaluator refreshed
from examples it selected itself can reproduce its own blind spots, and
one refreshed only on recent failures can forget distinctions needed for
older behaviors. The supervision loop needs anchors that stay fixed
across evaluator versions: outcome-linked examples spanning old and new
failure modes, selectively requested physical or human judgments, and a
protected success evaluation for disputed cases
(Section [4.3.2](#S4.SS3.SSS2 "4.3.2 Protecting the Judge ‣ 4.3 Keeping Improvement Safe ‣ 4 Challenges and Future Directions for Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")).
In the freeze–test–refresh–relabel sequence of
Section [4.2](#S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2 "When models and rewards fall behind. ‣ 4.2 Accumulating Improvement ‣ 4 Challenges and Future Directions for Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI"),
these anchors serve as the test. Versioning must connect each score to
the evaluator, evidence, and task definition that produced it.

A benchmark for evaluator refresh should therefore separate better
measurement from better supervision. With the learner, data, and update
budget fixed, it varies only the evaluator and its refresh rule, tests
judgments on independently selected old and new outcomes, and then
trains the same learner from each version’s labels and evaluates the
policies through protected physical outcomes. An evaluator counts as
progress only if it preserves the intended ordering of outcomes across
rounds and helps produce a better policy; fitting its refreshed labels
more accurately is not enough.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### 4.2 Accumulating Improvement

The gains reviewed in
Section [3](#S3 "3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
are often real but local. Consider the missed grasp once more. After the
robot learns to grasp reliably, its new successes may teach little that
it does not already know, and its contact model may not cover the faster
motions it now makes. A repaired grasp may expose a weakness in the
controller that executes it. A growing library of grasp skills may
become hard to search, and maintaining all of this machinery may cost
more than it saves. These failures map onto the conditions of
Section [2.2](#S2.SS2 "2.2 Defining Recursive Self-Improvement ‣ 2 Foundations of Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI").
Narrowing data strains _informative feedback_, outgrown models and
rewards reflect a lack of _robustness to distribution shift_, and a
moving bottleneck is a problem of _usability_. Accumulation strains both
usability and robustness to distribution shift, and infrastructure cost
bears on _continued practice_.
Table [14](#S4.T14 "Table 14 ‣ 4.2 Accumulating Improvement ‣ 4 Challenges and Future Directions for Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
lists the comparisons that bear most directly on each condition.
Carrying a benefit forward means that it remains useful for later
behavior or learning; performance need not grow at an accelerating rate.
Because recursion depends on gains that carry into the next round, each
of these stalls is also an obstacle to RSI.

Table 14: Comparisons that bear most directly on each condition.

##### When data stop teaching.

When autonomous imitation keeps only successful rollouts (filtered
behavior cloning), the next dataset increasingly reflects behavior that
the current policy can already produce. A higher success rate can then
raise the yield of accepted trajectories while each new trajectory
teaches less. The plateaus reported by [Mirchandani et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib199) are consistent with this pattern. PLD ([Xiao
et al., 2026a](#bib.bib305)) shows the complementary case: collectors
with equal success can differ in training value.

When success and training value diverge, choosing what to practice next
(a curriculum) must answer two questions. The first is _where_ another
trial is informative, which failure prediction and competence progress
answer differently. The second is _what supervision_ the selected state
needs. If an adequate recovery already lies within the range of behavior
the learner can produce, autonomous practice may expose it. If no useful
action is available, repeated failure adds little, and an expert
correction, a residual controller, or a new skill may be required.

The choice must also move with the policy. A state that once exposed a
useful error can become routine after correction, while better recovery
and reset mechanisms can make previously costly states reachable enough
to practice. Conversely, an irreversible or unreliable reset can make a
theoretically informative failure a poor use of a physical budget.
Collection, correction, and recovery should be reassessed together,
judged by the downstream learner’s gain and the physical cost.

##### When models and rewards fall behind.

A moving curriculum changes the distribution of situations in which the
next policy acts, and predictors and evaluators fitted to earlier rounds
can lose their footing. Two distinct forms of drift result. First, a
world model may have little _support_ (few comparable training examples)
for the improved policy’s actions and contacts, such as the faster
grasping motions it now makes, so optimization can favor trajectories
that look successful only because the prediction is wrong. Second, an
evaluator trained on earlier behavior may remain accurate on old
failures yet miss the subtler ones produced by a stronger policy.
Agreement between prediction and evaluation is weak evidence when both
are computed from the same imagined trajectory and share the same blind
spot about the physical world.

Existing methods respond at three different points. WISE ([Zhang et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib347)) restricts imagination to selected states and short
horizons, HaWMPO ([Chen et al., 2026j](#bib.bib49)) downweights rewards
from chunks it scores as hallucinated, and VLAW ([Guo et al.,
2026](#bib.bib90)) refits the world model on new physical rollouts.
Restriction and downweighting protect an update within the model’s
current support; refreshing attempts to enlarge that support. The
trade-off is temporal: a conservative imagination region can be reliable
now yet exclude the transitions required for the next improvement,
whereas expanding it consumes physical trials and helps only if
collection reaches the new policy’s relevant errors.

In PlayWorld ([Yin et al., 2026b](#bib.bib334)), prolonged fine-tuning
inside the model can keep improving the imagined reward while reducing
success on hardware, as the policy specializes to small prediction
mismatches, so even a comparatively accurate model remains open to
exploitation by optimization. Fresh physical rollouts act as an external
anchor for deciding when to stop, refresh, or distrust imagination.
Studies of generative models trained repeatedly on their own outputs
provide an adjacent warning: without enough real data, such loops can
progressively lose the tails of the data distribution ([Shumailov
et al., 2024](#bib.bib246)) or lose diversity ([Alemohammad et al.,
2024](#bib.bib5)), a coverage failure that any mixture of real and
imagined data must monitor.

Evaluator updates require a complementary timing rule. Combining
FIERCE’s per-round refresh, which already freezes a versioned evaluator
and relabels replay ([Tan et al., 2026b](#bib.bib263)), with PEBBLE’s
relabeling ([Lee et al., 2021](#bib.bib139)) suggests a
freeze–test–refresh–relabel sequence: keep feedback stable during an
update, test it against current outcomes, revise it when behavior
shifts, and make retained data consistent with the new version.

##### When bottlenecks move.

Every repair, including the repairs of prediction and feedback just
described, also changes what the next component receives. A bottleneck
moves when a previously adequate recipient becomes the dominant source
of end-to-end error. Two ablations expose such a recipient: in SILVR’s
simulated ablation ([Luo et al., 2026a](#bib.bib182)), a frozen action
translator limits what an updated video planner gains, and in
SHAPER ([Wang et al., 2026e](#bib.bib285)), skill guidance and the
harness that delivers it have non-additive effects. Neither study
follows the bottleneck across rounds, so the consequences below remain
hypotheses that a multi-round test would need to check.

When an execution module admits a wider range of behavior, the predictor
and evaluator should be retested on the newly reached states. A runtime
that rescues failures may hide from the learner the raw mistakes that
motivated the rescue, unless trajectories from before the recovery and
the corrections themselves are retained. A growing skill set forces the
harness to decide which repair applies and which evidence should be
preserved. A simulated study of 123 rounds of agentic skill
discovery ([Wang, 2026](#bib.bib279)) shows the resulting stall: changes
kept passing their tests, yet the target task never succeeded, because
perception could not represent the needed relation, learning
concentrated on the first step of long skill chains, and the agent
optimized the evaluator’s errors. A convincing test should evaluate the
full pipeline on the distribution reached after the repair, ablate the
receiving component, and inspect the next learning update, in addition
to rechecking the repaired component.

##### When knowledge is lost or misused.

As repairs accumulate, the usability problem becomes one of retention
and retrieval. _Retention_ asks whether an earlier behavior remains
available after the next update; _retrieval_ asks whether the right
behavior or record is selected under the present conditions. A system
can satisfy one without the other. An old skill may survive in the
weights yet be routed incorrectly, while a relevant trajectory may be
retrieved but decoded through an action interface whose coordinates have
changed. Lasting improvement must preserve content together with the
distinctions, interfaces, and applicability conditions that make it
usable.

Existing methods protect different parts of this path. Three methods
rehearse earlier behavior: Memory Anchors ([Du et al.,
2026](#bib.bib65)) through targeted replay, CIDER ([Li et al.,
2026d](#bib.bib148)) through distillation, and Dream to
Remember ([Tharwat et al., 2026](#bib.bib266)) inside a frozen world
model. Pretraining changes how much protection is needed. On LIBERO
suites in simulation, pretrained VLAs forget far less than small
policies trained from scratch, simple experience replay sometimes
removes forgetting, and skills that appear forgotten recover quickly
with finetuning ([Liu et al., 2026c](#bib.bib169)). Interpolating
finetuned weights with the pretrained ones retains generalist abilities
while learning a new task, in simulated and real experiments ([Yadav
et al., 2026](#bib.bib323)). Dream to Remember also learns new tasks in
imagination, but only where that model is accurate enough. ACCRUE ([Kim
et al., 2026](#bib.bib126)) instead carries lightweight actor–critic
networks across a task sequence, cutting real-robot training time for
later tasks by 31.0–68.5%, and FAN ([Hong et al., 2026a](#bib.bib101))
keeps the numerical meaning of retained actions fixed. These mechanisms
complement one another: better rehearsal cannot repair coordinate drift,
and stable coordinates do not decide which memory or skill applies.
Their evaluations also use bounded task streams, so retrieval from an
indefinitely growing repertoire is still to be tested.

External memories make that final problem explicit. Robo-Cortex ([Chan
et al., 2026](#bib.bib35)) consolidates episode histories into
retrievable principles and heuristics, whereas AllDayNav ([Yin et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib333)) stores temporal context and can replace or extend
visual memories as navigation experience accumulates. Their reported
system-level gains support the usefulness of maintained memory; a
general rule for detecting when a once-valid record has become stale has
yet to be developed.

Evaluation should expose each burden separately. The task suites of
Section [2.5](#S2.SS5 "2.5 Benchmarking Self-Improvement ‣ 2 Foundations of Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
provide breadth, but each still needs a continual-learning protocol on
top. After every update, the informative record is a matrix: performance
on the new task, on earlier tasks, on deliberately conflicting states,
and under shifted conditions in which stored knowledge may no longer
apply. The matrix separates forgetting, retrieval error, and stale
reuse, which a single final success rate would collapse together.

###### Surviving system changes.

Repair knowledge remains useful only while its applicability conditions
hold. A system revision can break these conditions at several
interfaces: a sensor or calibration change alters observations, a
controller or API change alters action semantics, and a new gripper
changes contact dynamics and reachable effects. Whether the change is
labeled “hardware” or “software” matters less than which relation the
retained artifact assumed. Replacing a gripper may invalidate a force
threshold or joint-space recovery while preserving the higher-level
strategy of releasing, retreating, and regrasping; renaming an API call
may break code while leaving the intended behavior realizable through a
new wrapper.

Maintenance has to operate on artifact-specific conditions. Policy
weights depend on observation and action representations and on
dynamics, and a learned evaluator depends on sensing and calibration. A
skill depends on its preconditions, effects, and available controller,
and code depends on APIs, schemas, timing, and permissions. A gate,
shield, or monitor depends on the policies and dynamics against which it
was validated. A single timestamp or confidence score for a whole memory
cannot show which assumption has become stale. Each retained change
should instead state its validity conditions: its required inputs,
action meanings, physical envelope, software dependencies, and the
evidence under which it last worked.

Those conditions support four different responses. An artifact can be
reused when its conditions still match, adapted when the task meaning is
preserved but an interface can be translated, selectively revalidated
when support is uncertain, or retired and rolled back when a required
effect is no longer realizable. The distinction also guards against a
misleading transfer claim. If a semantic recovery strategy succeeds on a
new gripper only after a newly engineered adapter reconstructs its
actions, the result tests the strategy and adapter together; the
original commands were not what transferred. Conversely, rejecting the
strategy because its old joint commands fail would overlook knowledge
that remains valid at a higher level of abstraction.

A benchmark could introduce declared changes to sensing, embodiment,
controller timing, APIs, and memory schemas, followed by gradual drift
in calibration or wear, and compare unconditional reuse, relearning from
scratch, and condition-aware adaptation or revalidation. Freezing the
retained artifact while varying the adapter, and then the reverse, would
separate semantic transfer from interface repair; the evaluation asks
whether the system identifies the invalidated condition and restores
held-out behavior without unsafe execution.

##### When costs outrun gains.

Building a world model, evaluator, reset routine, or repair library
consumes physical trials, engineering, supervision, and compute; reusing
it can save later trials but also requires storage, calibration, and
validation. Such an investment is worthwhile only if the artifact
remains useful long enough to repay its cost. If setup costs $`C_{0}`$
and reuse $`i`$ saves $`s_{i}`$ while incurring maintenance cost
$`m_{i}`$, all counted in one designated resource such as robot hours,
the investment pays back only when $`\sum_{i}(s_{i}-m_{i})>C_{0}`$
before a change in task, scene, or robot makes it obsolete (the payback
period). When several resources are involved, the criterion applies to
each separately rather than to their sum. This is a design criterion
that the surveyed studies do not yet estimate; reporting it alongside a
comparison would be a natural next measurement.

ENPIRE ([Xiao et al., 2026b](#bib.bib306)) provides a concrete but
bounded example: its safety, reset, and verification interfaces are
built once and reused during later policy search. In its fleet
experiments, scaling from one to eight agent–robot pairs reduces the
time to reach the target from roughly five to two hours on Push-T and
from more than 1.5 hours to about 40 minutes on pin insertion. The same
scaling study reports lower mean utilization per robot and
faster-than-linear growth in token consumption at eight agents; neither
a cost-optimal fleet size nor the rate at which costs are amortized
across tasks has been measured yet.

The appropriate repair depends on both expected reuse and the risk of
invalidation. A stable embodiment and a recurring family of tasks can
justify expensive retraining or reusable infrastructure, whereas an
imminent change in hardware or control interface favors a smaller,
reversible repair whose assumptions are easier to revalidate. The
resources involved are not interchangeable: more compute cannot undo
hardware wear, a faster fleet cannot replace a success evaluation that
no longer detects damage, and recovery can preserve access to trials
without making those trials free. Comparisons should hold the target
capability fixed and extend the cost accounting of
Section [4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Measuring Improvement ‣ 4 Challenges and Future Directions for Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
with robot utilization, the period over which the acquired capability is
reused, and retained performance after later updates.

###### Budgeting physical resources.

Beyond explaining why costs can outrun gains, the open problem is how to
allocate robot time, human attention, computation, reset effort, and
hardware wear over a deployment horizon. Simulation can replace some
hardware interaction but creates model-fitting and physical-validation
costs, and safety exposure should remain a constraint rather than be
traded against savings in time or computation.

An allocation decision should combine expected downstream learning,
frequency of reuse, maintenance and revalidation costs, and the
probability that a task or system revision invalidates the artifact. It
should also preserve option value: a reset capability, spare hardware
capacity, or a human escalation path can be worthwhile because it keeps
a future informative trial possible, even when it does not immediately
raise task success. Three efficiency indicators can complement the
causal tests: whether each round yields a gain, whether the gain arrives
faster than human-engineered iteration, and whether the cost of each
further gain, counted in robot time, attention, and wear, falls. A
falling cost can also come from reused infrastructure or easier tasks,
so it bears on the second recursive link only after the controlled
comparison of
Section [4.4](#S4.SS4.SSS0.Px6 "How to test recursion. ‣ 4.4 Making Improvement Recursive ‣ 4 Challenges and Future Directions for Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
has established that link.

A deployment-horizon benchmark could present a sequence of tasks,
failures, maintenance events, and system changes under finite resource
capacities, let a method choose at each stage whether to collect,
simulate, request supervision, build reusable infrastructure, revalidate
an artifact, or retire it, and compare a horizon-aware allocator with
myopic and fixed-budget schedules. Because no universal conversion rate
relates robot time, human time, compute, and wear, results should report
their trade-offs and their sensitivity to the assumed horizon rather
than a single cost.

### 4.3 Keeping Improvement Safe

For a robot that improves itself, safety preserves _continued practice_,
the opportunity on which another learning round depends: a robot that
damages its gripper or the object while practicing loses not only that
attempt but also the trials that would have followed. Each update can
also invalidate safety machinery built for the earlier system: an
updated controller may exceed the assumptions of a safety guard, and a
revised reset routine may no longer return the robot to a safe starting
state. A recursive system faces this at two levels, because a revised
learning procedure can also change what its safeguards must cover.
Surveys of safe reinforcement learning ([García and Fernández,
2015](#bib.bib82)) and of safe learning in control ([Brunke et al.,
2022](#bib.bib32)) catalog safeguards for collection, judgment, update,
and execution. Some mechanisms below have been tested in simulation,
formally, or on hardware; others are design requirements inferred from
the ways self-modification can fail.

#### 4.3.1 Keeping Practice Possible

Resetting is itself a capability that determines which experiments
remain possible, as Leave No Trace ([Eysenbach et al.,
2018](#bib.bib73)) and ReLMM ([Sun et al., 2022](#bib.bib254)) show.
Returning to an accessible starting state preserves the next experiment;
a human reset preserves it too, but by moving part of the work outside
the autonomous system. The resource that matters is safe access to an
informative state, which a count of rollouts measures poorly.

Keeping practice available also means maintaining the interfaces that
make another trial interpretable after wear, calibration drift, or
software change.

Self-modification creates two windows of safety exposure. During
improvement, harm can come from exploration, data collection, resets,
and candidate testing before an update is accepted. After an update is
accepted, the revised system can visit states or issue commands outside
the assumptions of its existing monitors and recovery routines. The two
windows can compound. A robot might first crush an object during
exploration. A revised reset might then leave the object where the
gripper cannot reach it, and an outcome detector that misses the damage
can retain that transition as useful experience. Safety is a property of
the whole loop of collection, judgment, update, and execution, not of
the deployed policy alone.

Existing methods protect different parts of this loop. Safe exploration
based on recoverability ([Moldovan and Abbeel, 2012](#bib.bib201))
formalizes safety as keeping, with a chosen probability, a route back to
a home state. Constrained policy optimization instead keeps policy
search near constraint satisfaction at every iteration ([Achiam et al.,
2017](#bib.bib1)). Recovery RL ([Thananjeyan et al., 2021](#bib.bib265))
learns this judgment from data, in simulation and on a surgical robot: a
safety critic estimates the chance of constraint violation, and a
learned recovery policy takes over when that chance crosses a threshold.
The Neural Simplex Architecture ([Phan et al., 2020](#bib.bib222))
switches to a baseline controller when a learned controller issues a
potentially unsafe input, retrains the learned controller online, and
returns control to it, in case studies on a ground rover and an
artificial pancreas. Learning-based control ([Brunke et al.,
2022](#bib.bib32)) instead constrains behavior relative to a model of
the dynamics and its uncertainty, for example through control barrier
functions ([Ames et al., 2019](#bib.bib7)) that keep the state in a
certified safe set; such guarantees remain conditional on assumptions
about state estimation, actuation, latency, and the operating envelope.
Each notion covers part of physical safety. Task success establishes
that an intended outcome occurred; failure detection covers only the
failure modes that a detector represents; and constraint satisfaction is
meaningful only relative to the specified constraint and model. A
self-modifying system can pass one of these tests while failing another.

The scope of a proposed modification determines which assumptions must
be revalidated. Policy learning changes which actions are taken, and
model-based practice can misestimate contact. A revision of memory,
runtime, or resets can alter recovery, and a revision of feedback can
change which failures are visible. For each candidate change, a record
of assumptions should note what changed, which safeguard depends on it,
what was rechecked, and which physical hazards remain unresolved.
Table [15](#S4.T15 "Table 15 ‣ 4.3.1 Keeping Practice Possible ‣ 4.3 Keeping Improvement Safe ‣ 4 Challenges and Future Directions for Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
applies this analysis to the objects that the four uses of retained
change can modify.

A recent survey of self-evolving humanoid robots ([Nguyen et al.,
2026](#bib.bib209)) similarly organizes safety around admissible
changes, verification gates, and boundaries for human oversight,
proposed as design principles for later testing; a survey of safety in
self-evolving language-model agents ([Chen et al., 2026c](#bib.bib39))
finds the evidence strongest for admission and local containment and
weakest for repairing what later versions inherit. A runtime guard can
reduce risk while one candidate executes, yet the update process is safe
only if admitting an update also revalidates the guard’s assumptions
after the change.
