#### 4.3.2 Protecting the Judge

A learning system can increase its recorded reward without improving the
intended physical outcome. Several mechanisms produce this gap, and each
needs its own defense. A misspecified objective rewards the wrong
behavior; an ordinary evaluator error mismeasures an otherwise relevant
outcome; specification gaming exploits an existing mismatch; and
tampering changes the process that generates the learning signal.
[Amodei et al. (2016)](#bib.bib8) separate problems such as side
effects, reward hacking, and costly supervision, while [Everitt et al.
(2021)](#bib.bib72) distinguish modifying the reward function from
modifying its inputs. Moving the camera so that a slipping grasp is
hidden affects the evaluator’s input, whereas editing the grasp-success
checker affects the evaluator itself.

Even ordinary evaluator errors matter once judged outcomes determine
which experience is kept. [Mirchandani et al. (2025)](#bib.bib199)
identify accurate success detection as part of the burden of designing
environments for autonomous robot data collection. A false positive can
place a failed contact in a dataset filtered for successes, after which
training can reproduce the pattern that was mislabeled as success. No
deliberate manipulation is required: a detector error at judgment time
becomes a data error at update time and can return as a behavioral error
in the next round. Versioning the evaluator together with the data it
labeled makes this propagation traceable, though finding the wrong
labels still requires an independent check. In SEAR’s simulated
self-exploration ([Wang et al., 2026h](#bib.bib290)), one agent run
saved a success verifier that was wrong on 91% of the 699 later rollouts
it declared successful, and the run ended at 4.6% success, against 15.5%
and 23.6% for sibling runs without it.

Once feedback itself can be revised, testing a candidate evaluator only
on outcomes or labels that it helped select becomes circular. Its
admission test needs a _protected success evaluation_: a source of
outcome judgments that the candidate update cannot also rewrite and that
remains informative about the relevant physical failure. Depending on
the hazard, this channel can combine held-out physical trials,
write-protected raw measurements, dedicated instrumentation, and human
review. ENPIRE’s verification services, which its coding agents cannot
modify, are one physical instance. A report should state which failure
modes the channel can reveal, which components it trusts, and which
blind spots remain.

#### 4.3.3 Admitting and Undoing Changes

An admission rule, or gate, turns protected evidence into a decision
about whether a candidate update should run, trading the risk of
accepting a harmful update against the cost of rejecting a useful one.
In the notation of
Section [2.2](#S2.SS2 "2.2 Defining Recursive Self-Improvement ‣ 2 Foundations of Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI"),
a confidence-based gate admits a candidate learner $`L^{\prime}`$ only
when a lower confidence bound on $`J(L^{\prime})-J(L)`$ is positive.
Batch RL formalized such gates early: high-confidence policy improvement
guarantees, at a chosen confidence level, that a returned policy
performs above a chosen lower bound ([Thomas et al.,
2015](#bib.bib267)), and SPIBB falls back on the baseline policy
wherever the data leave the estimate uncertain ([Laroche et al.,
2019](#bib.bib137)). In a constructed one-step pushing diagnostic, [Ma
and Wu (2026)](#bib.bib187) hold the stream of candidate updates fixed
and find that a gate based on a conservative range-based confidence
bound admits none of them, whereas a paired-binomial gate admits 31.6%
of them at 2,000 episodes per stage; in separate closed-loop runs,
always adopting the replay-trained update yields better learning than
either gated alternative. The evidence is analytical and synthetic; a
hardware safety comparison has yet to be run. Its broader lesson is that
admission should report both how well it controls errors and how many
learning opportunities it preserves at a stated interaction budget.

Robot-agent studies show the effect of the gate itself. When an
optimizer agent revises a robot agent’s harness, accepting every
revision degrades it within a few rounds, whereas a champion–challenger
rule raises held-out success on simulated LIBERO tasks from 51% to 67%
with 100 rollouts per round ([Wei et al., 2026b](#bib.bib298)). In
simulation, Robo-COP ([Zhang et al., 2026i](#bib.bib360)) reaches 73.8%
when it adopts a fine-tuned policy only after verifying an improvement,
against 65.8% for fine-tuning on a fixed schedule. A gate should also
report what a candidate loses: a net gain can hide cases that the
previous version solved, so a per-task regression check belongs beside
the aggregate test. RegenHarness ([Wang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib281))
makes such a protocol explicit for a robot-agent harness: a candidate
change to context rules, task templates, routing, or recovery policies
is accepted only if it preserves safety and evidence contracts, passes
designated regression checks, improves a predeclared metric, and
receives release authorization. The updater cannot weaken its own
acceptance rule. Its real quadruped deployment documents the runtime
rather than measuring gains from revision.

Once a candidate is admitted, runtime mechanisms limit what each trial
can do, and they intervene at different points. The shield of [Alshiekh
et al. (2018)](#bib.bib6) corrects actions that would violate a property
stated in temporal logic, a formal language for requirements over time
such as “never enter this region”. The learned monitor of [Liu et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib168) instead predicts states that are out of
distribution or likely to fail and requests human oversight. The first
is conditional on a specification and a model of the environment; the
second is conditional on learned dynamics, failure labels, and the
coverage of deployment. Neither protects against a hazard absent from
its representation.

Other mechanisms move the check earlier or broaden the boundary around
execution. VASO ([Yang et al., 2026e](#bib.bib332)) checks whole plans,
model-checking skill-based plans against temporal specifications and
using counterexamples to revise reusable skill contracts; GLIDE ([Song
et al., 2026c](#bib.bib250)) checks single commands, filtering
teleoperation and policy commands through task-specific executable
guardrails; and PhyAgentOS ([Liu et al., 2026h](#bib.bib174)) wraps
whole supervised sessions in compatibility checks before execution,
verification, monitoring, and evidence collection. Safe online system
identification ([Zhang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib346)) shows the value of
stating assumptions precisely: its informative manipulator trajectories
respect modeled input, state, and collision constraints, while its
bounds on estimated parameters assume bounded sensor noise. Formal
compliance, learned failure prediction, command filtering, and runtime
mediation provide different kinds of evidence, and none translates
directly into an unconditional probability of physical safety.

Systems that change their own software require a further boundary around
authority. An updater should receive only the tool, file, network, and
actuation permissions needed for the current experiment, while an
independently controlled deployment service retains emergency stops,
workspace limits, safety-critical calibration, and the authority to
approve promotion. Each proposed change needs a provenance record
linking the generating model, the prompt or memory used, the code diff,
the data and evaluator versions, the test results, and the decision. A
correct outcome does not show that each action rested on evidence
gathered first; [Lin et al. (2026)](#bib.bib163) make this point for
tool-using software agents by auditing trajectories against a
provenance-bound evidence ledger. The checker can still err, but no
single permission path can then silently rewrite both the candidate and
every mechanism intended to assess it.

Promotion can then proceed from sandboxed tests of interfaces and logic
to guarded physical trials within a declared operating envelope. Each
stage should record which assumptions it tested and which physical
unknowns remain; success in simulation alone cannot establish contact
safety or hardware compatibility. Recovery also has to respect
dependencies among components. A previous grasp policy may no longer
work with a revised model, memory schema, or runtime, so rollback should
restore a compatible versioned bundle rather than an isolated
checkpoint. Even such a rollback restores only computational state.
Trial limits and a stopping mechanism are still required before an
update is admitted, because no rollback can undo a crushed object or a
damaged gripper.

#### 4.3.4 Placing Human Oversight

Gates and safeguards face a practical dilemma: continuous human
monitoring limits scale, but removing supervision leaves unfamiliar
failures without a reliable response. Human attention is most
informative where automation lacks either a safe action or trustworthy
evidence: before an irreversible contact, at a state the policy has not
been trained on, when outcome signals disagree, or when a
safety-relevant component is proposed for revision. These situations
assign the human different roles: taking control prevents harm, a
corrective action supplies a learning target, an audit adjudicates an
outcome, and an approval authorizes a change. Recording these roles
separately matters, because one intervention can otherwise be counted
simultaneously as safety, as training data, and as evidence of autonomy.
Interruptions can also bias what is learned: an agent rewarded for
finishing a task may learn to avoid being stopped, and safe
interruptibility requires that learning neither seek nor avoid
interruptions, a property that off-policy learners such as Q-learning
already have and Sarsa can be given ([Orseau and Armstrong,
2016](#bib.bib217)).

Timing determines whether an intervention supplies that information.
HIL-SERL ([Luo et al., 2025](#bib.bib184)) uses demonstrations and human
corrections during real-world RL, intervening often early in training
and less as performance improves. ThriftyDAgger ([Hoque et al.,
2022a](#bib.bib103)) requests help at states that are novel to a policy
ensemble or risky under a learned estimate of task success, with
thresholds set from an intervention budget. SAGE ([Hu et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib107)) makes the threshold itself adaptive, so that
predicted risk, uncertainty, and novelty decide when an expert policy
takes over. These illustrate two allocation strategies, operator
judgment and learned triage; neither is shown to detect every unsafe
state. A late intervention may rescue the object without preventing a
dangerous contact, whereas an overly conservative trigger can replace so
much autonomy that the learner learns little about the limits of its
competence.

A rescue also changes how the episode should be learned from. If an
autonomous grasp starts to slip and a person then completes the lift,
crediting the final success to the entire trajectory can reinforce the
very action that required correction. TORL-VLA ([Zheng et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib367)) addresses this case in real-robot experiments with
an intervention-censored critic, which prevents success achieved after
an intervention from being credited to the policy’s actions before the
takeover. The broader requirement is a record of who was in control:
each transition should identify who acted, why control changed, and
which later outcomes may legitimately supervise the preceding decision.

Fewer takeovers can coexist with more oversight overall, because control
effort may fall while learning effort (demonstrations, corrections, and
outcome labels) or assurance effort (audits, calibration, checker
maintenance, and approvals) rises. Reports should separate these costs
and state the trigger, who has authority to respond, and how quickly the
supervisor can act. The broader survey of recursive self-improvement by
[Chen et al. (2026d)](#bib.bib41) likewise treats the closing of the
loop as a continuum and identifies evaluation and the setting of
research direction as persistent human bottlenecks. For physical
systems, a meaningful claim about autonomy names which decisions became
reliably automated and where in the loop supervision moved.

Proposing a change, admitting it, executing it, and judging its outcome
can be run by the same people, as long as the four steps do not all
depend on the same mutable component or unprotected signal and each
stage retains evidence or control capable of exposing and containing
failure in the preceding one.

#### 4.3.5 Revalidating Safety Across Generations

Admission and rollback act on one candidate at a time; a system that
revises its own learning procedure must also ask whether the evidence
behind its safeguards survives the revision. Three questions recur.
First, does earlier safety evidence still apply? A guard validated for
one controller, action normalization, or reset routine holds only for
what it was validated on. FAN shows that updating action-normalization
statistics shifts the coordinates shared by training and execution, so a
bound stated in the old coordinates would need rechecking, and
Table [15](#S4.T15 "Table 15 ‣ 4.3.1 Keeping Practice Possible ‣ 4.3 Keeping Improvement Safe ‣ 4 Challenges and Future Directions for Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
lists how other revisions can invalidate safety assumptions. Each
generation therefore needs a record of which checks were run against
which component versions, and a rule that marks dependent checks as
stale when those versions change.

Second, who may change the safety boundary? ENPIRE builds its safety,
reset, and verification services in a human-guided stage and exposes
them as interfaces that its coding agents cannot modify, and
RegenHarness forbids its updater to weaken its own acceptance rule; the
same separation should extend to the improver, so that a revision of the
learning procedure cannot also relax the checks that judge it.

Third, how are regressions across versions and bodies caught? A net gain
can hide cases that the previous version solved, and a hardware change
such as a replaced gripper can invalidate behavior that no software
rollback restores; regression suites carried across generations and
rerun after hardware changes keep earlier competence and safety margins
visible. These requirements are inferred from the reviewed failures;
testing them over several generations of a self-revising physical system
is part of the open problem of surviving system changes
(Section [4.2](#S4.SS2.SSS0.Px4.SPx1 "Surviving system changes. ‣ When knowledge is lost or misused. ‣ 4.2 Accumulating Improvement ‣ 4 Challenges and Future Directions for Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")).

##### Beyond safety.

Self-improving robots also raise questions that safety engineering does
not settle. Fleet learning gathers experience in homes and workplaces,
as when OpenBot-Fleet ([Müller et al., 2024](#bib.bib202)) uploads data
from user-operated robots, so consent, retention, and access to recorded
scenes become part of the design of the learning loop. When a robot
revises its own learning procedure, responsibility for a harmful update
must also stay traceable; the provenance records and separated authority
described above serve accountability as well as safety.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### 4.4 Making Improvement Recursive

A recursive improver must decide what to repair and what to try before
it can learn from its repairs. This subsection takes these capabilities
in turn, from diagnosis and experiment choice to transferable repair
knowledge, and then designs the test that would show the loop closing.

##### Finding the bottleneck.

The agenda begins with diagnosis because changing the wrong component
consumes physical trials and can obscure the evidence needed for the
next attempt. The same observed failure can have several causes, as the
missed grasp of
Section [1](#S1 "1 Introduction ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
shows, so a failure label alone cannot determine which repair to choose.
Calling a component the bottleneck therefore states a hypothesis to be
tested against other, interacting explanations; logs can narrow those
explanations but rarely determine which change will improve downstream
behavior, and
Table [16](#S4.T16 "Table 16 ‣ Finding the bottleneck. ‣ 4.4 Making Improvement Recursive ‣ 4 Challenges and Future Directions for Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
separates evidence that supports a diagnosis before intervention from
comparisons that test a candidate repair after intervention.

Table 16: Checks before repair and comparisons after intervention.

Physical traces make this inference harder because they are partial and
often censored by safety mechanisms. An intervention may prevent the
failure that would have revealed the weakness, while the final rescued
success may conceal which autonomous transition required correction. A
diagnostic trace should align observations, proposed actions, executed
actions, any shield or human modification, feedback versions, and
intervention timing. Unobserved signals should stay marked as unknown,
never counted as evidence that a component worked. The _bottleneck_ is
the component hypothesized to limit the next improvement, given the
available repairs; diagnosing it does not presuppose a single
independent root cause.

Failure explanation is a natural starting point. REFLECT ([Liu et al.,
2023c](#bib.bib175)) summarizes multisensory robot experience
hierarchically and asks a language model to explain failures and plan
corrections, and AHA ([Duan et al., 2025](#bib.bib67)) fine-tunes a
vision-language model on procedurally perturbed demonstrations to detect
and explain manipulation failures. Both explain a failure from the
recorded episode alone. A diagnostic system should go further, keeping
competing explanations ranked and choosing a small, safe probe expected
to separate them before attempting a costly repair. A concrete benchmark
could inject matched policy, model, evaluator, and interface faults that
produce similar terminal outcomes within the same task family. Single
faults would test basic identification; unseen combinations and
intervention-censored traces would test whether the method preserves
uncertainty when causes interact or evidence is missing. Fault injection
supplies controlled causal labels but not full realism, so the resulting
repair choices should also be tested on held-out, naturally occurring
hardware failures. Evaluation should measure calibrated cause rankings,
information gained per probe, and, most importantly, whether the
selected repair improves downstream behavior from matched starting
points and physical budgets. This last test separates useful diagnosis
from classification that merely names the injected fault.

##### Choosing the next experiment.

While several causes remain plausible, the most diagnostic experiment
and the most useful learning experience can differ. Suppose a grasp
failure could reflect either a missing recovery action or an incorrect
contact model. Repeating the contact with additional force sensing may
separate those explanations, but evidence of a contact-model error helps
only if a model update can represent the discrepancy and a later learner
can use the revised prediction. An expert correction supplies an
immediately usable action target, yet may leave the contact-model error
unresolved. An experiment is useful for learning only if an available
update method can use the evidence it provides, so its value depends on
which uncertainty it reduces and whether the resulting update improves
behavior.

An experiment also incurs reset, wear, intervention, and safety costs
immediately, whereas its learning benefit appears only after updating
and redeployment. Some informative states cannot be revisited safely,
yet a promising repair may need one. A staged selector could first use
stored traces, counterfactual replay, or short model-based probes, then
request new contact or correction only while the remaining explanations
would lead to different usable updates. Cheap probes narrow the question
but cannot resolve a physical distinction that their data or model
omits.

A benchmark for this problem should compare joint experiment–update
selection with fixed collection, information-gain-only selection, and a
sequential baseline that diagnoses first and chooses an update
afterward, scoring held-out behavioral improvement rather than predicted
information gain under the reporting rules of
Section [4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Measuring Improvement ‣ 4 Challenges and Future Directions for Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI").
Ablating either the predicted information gain or the predicted
usability of the evidence would show which part of the joint decision
matters.

##### Transferring repair knowledge.

Recursion requires retaining what was learned from a repair, not only
the repaired policy. A stored edit without its applicability conditions
supports patch reuse, and a searcher that keeps rediscovering edits
repeats a search rather than learning from earlier repairs.

Learning such knowledge requires histories that expose both success and
failure. The same slip penalty can help one grasping policy and harm
another because their exploration differs; a code repair can depend on
an API, timing convention, sensor, or control rate. Each record should
connect the proposed explanation and unresolved alternatives, attempted
change, starting competence, component and interface versions, data and
feedback, physical conditions, resources spent, and downstream successes
or regressions. Failed revisions do more than serve as negative
examples: they identify missing prerequisites or incorrect causal
explanations. Selectively recording only accepted patches would make an
editor appear more reliable while removing the evidence needed to decide
when not to reuse them.

The main open problem is how to use accumulating real-robot revision
histories to learn a procedure improver that transfers across failure
types, and to verify that it also helps produce its own next
improvement. If what is learned does not transfer beyond near-duplicates
of past failures, repair knowledge amounts to a library of patches, and
the two-round test below reduces to a test of reuse. The improver must
separate transferable gains from those due to extra data, a stronger
starting policy, or a changed apparatus, and recognize when to reuse an
earlier repair, adapt it, or seek a different explanation. Benchmark
tasks should vary starting competence, feedback versions, interfaces,
and physical conditions while keeping tools, opportunities, and budgets
matched. Direct retrieval of an old patch should be reported as reuse; a
transferable repair principle should pass both comparisons of
Figure [9](#S4.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ How to test recursion. ‣ 4.4 Making Improvement Recursive ‣ 4 Challenges and Future Directions for Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
on held-out failure families.

##### Testing recursive improvement.

Can a system learn from attempted repairs to improve the way it produces
further improvements? The two links of
Section [2.2](#S2.SS2 "2.2 Defining Recursive Self-Improvement ‣ 2 Foundations of Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
describe a causal dependence across revisions, which no count of mutable
components, checkpoints, or autonomous steps can establish.
Section [4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Measuring Improvement ‣ 4 Challenges and Future Directions for Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
sets out the judgments that a recursive claim must keep apart; the
two-round test below would isolate either link for a learning procedure.

##### Where recursion could start.

Each of the four routes can supply the object of a recursive test: a
rule for changing that route, together with records of how earlier
changes fared.

For _policies_, the natural rule to revise is the one that chooses which
experience to collect. A criticality model already steers collection
toward likely failures and, in two simulated multi-round runs, is
retrained on the current policy’s rollouts each round; a recursive
version would also learn, from which collections taught later learners,
how to revise that criterion.

For _world models_, the rule decides when a model may judge. A learned
model is the closest physical counterpart of the executable tests that
make digital RSI cheap, because it can screen candidate changes before
hardware trials, but its judgments must themselves be checked. On a
physical arm, a world-model judge fine-tuned only on successes scores
most held-out failing sequences as success-like, and fine-tuning on
execution-checked counterfactual failures reduces this sharply ([Xu
et al., 2026c](#bib.bib318)). A recursive version would learn from such
mismatches how to refresh the judge, so that each refresh leaves fewer
errors for the next.

For _external knowledge_, the rule decides what to keep from a repair.
Memories, skills, and code can store repair knowledge in inspectable
form, with the applicability conditions that the preceding paragraphs
ask each record to carry, and a frozen memory snapshot directly supplies
the control described below.

For the _learning procedure_, the rule is the improver itself, such as a
reward editor or the procedure that trains a skill-library editor. The
test below starts there, because Eureka and PRACTICE already supply
fixed-improver baselines. Across the four routes, what differs is where
repair knowledge lives and how it can be frozen, not what the test must
show.

##### How to test recursion.

A bounded test can focus on reward construction, as in the missed-grasp
example of
Section [3.3](#S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1 "What would count as a better improver. ‣ 3.3 Improving the Improver ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI"),
or on skill-library editing
(Figure [9](#S4.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ How to test recursion. ‣ 4.4 Making Improvement Recursive ‣ 4 Challenges and Future Directions for Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")),
for which existing systems already supply baselines. Eureka is a reward
improver whose knowledge does not change, and PRACTICE is a learned
skill editor whose own improver, the staged procedure that trains it, is
fixed. The proposed test extends the matched downstream comparison of
Figure [8](#S3.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ 3.2 Improving Learning Procedures ‣ 3 Mechanisms toward Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
from a revised procedure to the improver that produces it by comparing a
learned improver before and after it learns from earlier repairs:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 9: A proposed test of the two links of recursive self-improvement
(R1 and R2). In R2, the updated improver revises itself with frozen or
acquired knowledge, producing the control or next improver,
respectively. Each then revises a learning procedure, which is tested
through fresh matched learners under a common, protected outcome check;
the next improver must beat both the control and the updated improver;
for the updated improver, its learner from R1 serves as the baseline.
The R2 control assumes that the acquired knowledge can be withheld
without changing the parent improver, as with a memory snapshot; the
count of four hardware-trained learners per seed assumes that one
candidate per improver survives screening.

- •
  Hold the new problem common. Give both versions the same new failure
  histories, tools, objectives, and revision budget. Let them generate
  or select candidate learning procedures, rather than only task
  controllers.
- •
  Test what those procedures teach. Apply the candidates to matched
  learners and evaluate common physical outcomes. Report the cost of
  updating the improver separately.
- •
  Follow the improver’s next revision. Given common new repair
  histories, let the updated improver propose a revision of itself and
  compare the result both with the unrevised improver and with a control
  revision of the same improver proposed with its earlier knowledge
  frozen. Repeating the first two tests on the resulting improvers links
  further gains to what was learned.

The first two steps test the first link and the third tests the second,
as stated by the R1 and R2 inequalities of
Section [2.2](#S2.SS2 "2.2 Defining Recursive Self-Improvement ‣ 2 Foundations of Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
(Figure [9](#S4.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ How to test recursion. ‣ 4.4 Making Improvement Recursive ‣ 4 Challenges and Future Directions for Physical RSI ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI"));
retention, performance under changed conditions, and sustainable
resource use decide whether the relation is useful beyond a local
controlled test. SEAR ([Wang et al., 2026h](#bib.bib290)) already
supplies benchmark controls for such tests, separating retained
experience from repeated attempts, task familiarity, privileged state,
larger budgets, and chance.

##### What the test must control.

A successor can score higher because of accumulated experience or a
stronger starting system rather than a better improvement mechanism, as
a concurrent survey also notes ([Zhou et al., 2026a](#bib.bib371)).
Three details decide whether the test is informative. First, freezing
must match the form of the improver’s knowledge: a parametric improver
is compared with its earlier checkpoint, a retrieval-based improver with
its earlier memory snapshot, and an improver whose knowledge lives in
code or prompts with their earlier versions, while the base model,
tools, and budget stay the same. This suffices for R1, but R2 also
requires the control revision to start from the same parent. That holds
when the acquired knowledge can be withheld without changing the rest of
the improver, as with a memory snapshot or separable code or prompts;
when the knowledge lives in the improver’s weights, restoring the
earlier checkpoint also changes the parent, so the R2 control for a
parametric improver needs a design of its own. Second, the new failure
families must be held out from everything the improver has learned from;
otherwise the comparison measures memorization. Third, the physical cost
should be staged: candidate procedures can be screened in simulation or
on stored traces, so that hardware trials go to matched learners for the
few candidates that survive. With one survivor per improver, the two
comparisons need four hardware-trained learners per seed, because the
updated improver’s learner from the first comparison also serves as the
parent baseline of the second: about 1,200 refinement rollouts at
FIERCE’s per-condition budget, excluding evaluation, resets, and
repetition across failure families. Digital precedents run close
analogues of both comparisons when evaluation is cheap; the physical
version adds protected outcomes and a matched downstream learner.
SpecRSI’s same-artifact comparison, which runs the original and the
updated improver on one released artifact, is a digital instance of this
control.

Three near-term programs follow from the agenda. First, combine
cross-component diagnosis with joint experiment–update selection under
matched multi-resource budgets, so that the correct repair and the cost
of identifying it both determine success. Second, test versioned
evaluators and repair knowledge on held-out failures and declared
hardware or software changes, using protected outcome checks to separate
transfer from drift. Third, connect these tests across at least two
causally isolated procedure-revision rounds and report their full
acquisition, maintenance, and revalidation costs.

## 5 Conclusion

This survey examined how robots that improve from physical experience
can move toward recursive self-improvement, in which a system improves
not only its behavior but also the process by which it improves. We
positioned RSI within robot learning: reinforcement learning,
self-training, continual learning, meta-learning, and AutoML say how
updates are computed or what they must cope with, whereas a ladder of
claims states what an experiment shows to have improved. Along that
ladder, we reviewed how physical experience improves policies, world
models, and knowledge, the learning procedures that produce them, and
the improver that revises those procedures. What limits a robot’s next
improvement (RQ1) is rarely visible in a terminal outcome; it is a
hypothesis about missing experience, supervision, optimization, action
generation, interfaces, or retention, to be tested by intervention
rather than inferred from data volume or component accuracy. The changes
that address it (RQ2) are kept in policies, world models, external
knowledge, or the learning procedure, and they build on one another
(RQ3) only under four conditions: feedback addresses remaining learning
needs, the receiving component can use the change, its value survives
changes in tasks or hardware, and continued practice remains safe and
affordable. Physical constraints (RQ4) act through all four: incomplete
sensing limits what a signal can distinguish; embodiment interfaces
limit what a recipient can execute; wear, calibration drift, and
hardware changes drive distribution shift; and reset, safety, and cost
bound continued practice.

Existing studies, concentrated in manipulation, support behavioral
improvement, later-learning benefits, and procedure improvement. Some
systems also change their improver’s knowledge or tools, but no physical
study reviewed here has yet isolated a gain attributable to recursion,
which requires a controlled comparison against a version of the improver
whose acquired knowledge is frozen. These answers remain provisional,
because the four conditions are overlapping diagnostic lenses rather
than independently validated constructs and much of the evidence comes
from recent preprints with few training runs or trials.

Digital agents already supply mechanisms for revising their own code and
tools. Whether these mechanisms work with physical experience and under
physical constraints depends on the open problems identified here:
evaluation on tasks the revising system cannot tune against, with
matched learners for claims beyond behavior; gains that keep
accumulating as data stop teaching and bottlenecks move; practice that
stays safe while the procedure governing it changes; and an improver
that learns to find bottlenecks, choose experiments, and transfer repair
knowledge. Physical recursive self-improvement will be demonstrated not
when a robot changes many times, but when knowledge of why one repair
worked causally improves how the next repair is made, and when that
improved capability, applied to new evidence, helps improve itself again
without losing the ability to keep learning. Even a robot that becomes
measurably better at rewriting its own recipe for a single family of
failures would give the first such evidence.

## Appendix A Extended Landscape of Physical Self-Improvement

This appendix extends the coverage of the mechanisms reviewed in the
main text.
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Reported Outcomes and Experimental Context ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
records selected numerical outcomes and their denominators, and
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Glossary ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
collects the terms used throughout.

Table [17](#A1.T17 "Table 17 ‣ Appendix A Extended Landscape of Physical Self-Improvement ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
shows, stage by stage, what people and systems contribute to the
reviewed loops.
Table [18](#A1.T18 "Table 18 ‣ Appendix A Extended Landscape of Physical Self-Improvement ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
identifies the support for cross-domain interpretations. Manipulation
supplies detailed component and downstream comparisons; navigation,
locomotion, flight, and laboratories contribute particular reuse,
adaptation, and experiment-selection mechanisms.
Table [19](#A1.T19 "Table 19 ‣ Appendix A Extended Landscape of Physical Self-Improvement ‣ Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI")
then extends the system coverage with policy post-training, autonomous
resets, fleets, dynamics adaptation, reusable memory, continual
learning, and contact-aware feedback. It includes both system-generated
and expert-provided experience and distinguishes training from
evaluation settings.
